What are my options for selling a house in Federal Way?

Most Federal Way owners choose among a listing with an agent, a sale they run themselves, and a direct purchase by a buyer who pays without a mortgage. The right one depends on the condition of the house, how soon you need to move, and what you still owe on it.

  • Agent listing: You prepare the house, allow showings and negotiate whatever repairs the buyer's inspection turns up. It reaches the widest pool of buyers and asks the most patience.
  • Selling it yourself: You set the price, market the house and handle the paperwork, including the seller disclosure statement that Washington requires for improved residential property unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt.
  • Direct cash purchase: The buyer is not waiting on a lender, so the sale does not hinge on loan approval. Compare the written offer with what you would net after the loan payoff, taxes and any repairs you would otherwise pay for.

What is Federal Way like, and why does it matter for a sale?

Federal Way sits in the southwest corner of King County, about 25 miles south of Seattle. The city covers 23.72 square miles, 22.32 of them land, and it holds lakes such as Steel Lake and Lake Killarney. Its name came from a school district formed in 1929, which in turn took the name of U.S. Route 99, today's Pacific Highway South.

The city is young on paper. Voters turned down incorporation in 1971, 1981 and 1985 before approving it on February 28, 1990. Interstate 5 opened through the area in October 1962 and turned it into a commuter community for Seattle workers. Weyerhaeuser opened its headquarters complex east of I-5 in 1971 and announced in 2014 that it would leave, and World Vision's U.S. headquarters is also here.

Wikipedia describes the city as marked by 1990s semi-urban development: landscaped apartment complexes and shopping centers, with The Commons at Federal Way as the only indoor mall, at South 320th Street and SR 99. Parks give some neighborhoods their pull. Steel Lake Park sits on South 312th Street, Dash Point State Park is the only developed waterfront park inside the city, and West Hylebos Wetlands Park holds the Barker Cabin, built in 1883 and the oldest known building in Federal Way.

Summers are warm and dry, and no monthly average temperature tops 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit. A few neighborhoods to the east, including Star Lake, Camelot, Lakeland and Jovita, were named potential annexation areas, and residents of the East Federal Way area rejected annexation by 66 to 34 percent on August 21, 2007. Confirm that your parcel is inside city limits before you contact the Permit Center.

How much excise tax will I owe when I sell in Federal Way?

The seller owes it. Washington's real estate excise tax is the seller's obligation under RCW 82.45.080, and the Department of Revenue says it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, whether or not the deed is recorded that day. A deeded sale of a Federal Way house is reported to King County, where the city lies.

The state portion is graduated. Under the thresholds now posted by the Department of Revenue, the first $525,000 of the price is taxed at 1.1 percent, the slice up to $1,525,000 at 1.28 percent, the slice up to $3,025,000 at 2.75 percent, and anything above that at 3 percent. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the cut points move to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. A local rate is added on top, so ask your escrow officer for the figure that applies to your parcel.

As an example, a sale at the $552,800 median value would carry about $6,131 in state tax: $5,775 on the first $525,000 and about $356 on the rest. The tax must be paid within one month of the sale, or penalty and interest begin, and unpaid tax can become a lien on the property. Ask for the excise tax to appear as its own line on the settlement statement.

Do I need a permit or approval before selling a Federal Way house?

The City of Federal Way Permit Center handles building, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, demolition and fire prevention permits, along with land use and sign permits. It is the office to ask about repairs you plan to finish before a sale, or about work a previous owner may have done without a permit.

  • Phone and email: 253-835-2607 or permitcenter@federalwaywa.gov.
  • Hours: 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. The center is closed to the public on Wednesdays and on city holidays, including the day after Thanksgiving.
  • Applications: Anything that needs review is submitted electronically after you request a Document Upload Link, which can take a few days. Residential electrical, mechanical and plumbing permits can be applied for online through My Building Permit.

The city also warns that it will not unexpectedly ask for payment by wire transfer based on an email. If a message claims to be from the city and asks for money, call the Permit Center before you send anything. For parcel numbers, use the city's maps, the King County Parcel Viewer, or ask the Permit Center.

How do roads, transit and schools shape buyer interest in Federal Way?

Federal Way is served by Interstate 5 at the 348th Street, 320th Street and 272nd Street exits and by State Route 99, the Pacific Highway. The Federal Way Transit Center on 23rd Avenue South is served by King County Metro, Pierce Transit and Sound Transit Express, and the Link light rail extension to Federal Way Downtown station opened in December 2025. Average travel time to work is 32.1 minutes, so access to the freeway and the station is a real selling point for commuters.

Public schools come from Federal Way Public Schools, the district that formed in 1929 as School District No. 210. When you describe your house to a buyer, name the nearest park, the nearest I-5 exit and the walk or drive to the station.

What should I check before I accept an offer on my Federal Way house?

  • Get the offer in writing, with the price, the closing date and who pays each closing cost.
  • Request a payoff statement from your lender so you know the exact balance.
  • Ask the buyer for proof of funds, and ask whether the offer depends on repairs or an inspection.
  • Estimate your excise tax with the rates above and ask escrow for the local rate.
  • Find out whether the buyer expects the house to be emptied, and by what date.
  • Compare the net figure from each route, not the headline price alone.

More questions about Federal Way, WA

Who pays the real estate excise tax on a house sale in Federal Way?

The seller. RCW 82.45.080 makes the tax the seller's obligation, and the Department of Revenue notes that if the seller does not pay, the buyer becomes responsible. Unpaid tax can create a lien on the property.

When are property taxes due on a Federal Way house?

First-half taxes are due by April 30 and second-half taxes by October 31. RCW 84.56.020 makes the county treasurer the collector, so Federal Way owners pay through King County. Ask the county for the current statement on your parcel.

Which county is Federal Way in?

King County. The city lies in the southwest corner of the county, about 25 miles south of Seattle, so deeds, excise tax affidavits and property tax bills for a Federal Way home go through King County offices.

How do I find my parcel number in Federal Way?

Use the City's maps or the King County Parcel Viewer, or contact the Permit Center at 253-835-2607 or permitcenter@federalwaywa.gov. You will need the parcel number for permit questions and for title work.

Do I have to give a buyer a seller disclosure statement?

Usually yes. RCW 64.06.020 requires the seller of improved residential property to deliver a completed disclosure statement within five business days after a written contract is accepted, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt. The buyer has three business days after delivery to rescind.

A sale to a cash buyer is typically the quickest path, since it removes the buyer's mortgage approval and appraisal from the schedule. A listing can still bring a higher price if the house shows well and you can wait for the right offer.

Yakima is the seat of Yakima County and the 11th most populous city in Washington, in the Upper Valley of Yakima County, about 60 miles southeast of Mount Rainier. The Census Bureau estimates 97,458 residents as of July 1, 2025. West Valley and Terrace Heights are unincorporated suburbs that are treated as part of greater Yakima, so confirm whether your address is inside city limits before you check any city rule.

The Yakama people were the first known inhabitants of the valley. The U.S. Army established Fort Simcoe in 1856 after the Yakima War, and Yakima County was created in 1867. The city's name comes from the Yakama Nation, whose reservation lies south of town, and the Yakama Nation's government and enterprises remain among the area's larger employers.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table reports the following for Yakima city.

What drives the Yakima housing market?

Agriculture does. The Yakima Valley produces apples, peaches, pears, cherries and melons, along with peppers, corn and beans, and as of 2011 it grew 77 percent of the hops harvested in the United States. Many residents came to the valley to pick, process, market and support that farm economy.

The city's 2022 financial report, summarized on Wikipedia, lists the largest employers:

  • Yakima Valley Memorial Hospital, 2,500 employees
  • Walmart (Yakima, Sunnyside and Grandview), 1,700
  • Yakima School District, 1,594
  • Zirkle Fruit and Washington Fruit and Produce, 1,500 each
  • Yakama Nation Government Operations, 1,289

Downtown Yakima was long the retail hub, but the regional retail core has moved to Union Gap, where a renovated mall and new stores opened.

How does Yakima's climate affect a house?

Yakima has a cold semi-arid climate, with a location in a rain shadow that holds precipitation to about 8 inches a year. Annual snowfall averages 21.6 inches, mostly in December and January, and the average last freeze of spring comes on May 13, with the first freeze of fall around September 30.

Summers are hot. The city averages 40.2 afternoons a year at 90 degrees or higher and 5.7 at 100 degrees or higher, and it reached 113 degrees on June 29, 2021. Day-to-night swings in July average nearly 35 degrees. Roofing, attic insulation, cooling equipment and exterior paint carry the load from those swings, so any receipts or warranties for them are worth collecting before you list. Yakima sits at 1,095 feet above sea level.

Which schools and highways matter to Yakima buyers?

The Yakima School District runs four high schools in the city: Davis High School, Eisenhower High School, Stanton Academy and Yakima Online High School. West Valley High School is in the West Valley School District, and East Valley High School, just east of Terrace Heights, is in the East Valley School District.

Interstate 82 is the main freeway, linking Yakima to Ellensburg and the Tri-Cities with onward routes to Seattle and Oregon. U.S. Route 12 crosses the north of the city and joins I-82 and U.S. Route 97 on the east side. State Route 24 ends in Yakima and leads to Moxee and the farm areas to the east, while State Route 821 follows the Yakima River canyon toward Ellensburg. The average commute for city workers is 17.8 minutes.

Which repairs need a permit in Yakima?

The city's Code Administration office explains this on its permit process page. Some jobs can be applied for online without plan review:

  • Same-for-same plumbing and mechanical change-outs
  • Residential reroofs that are tear off and reroof only
  • Water and sewer line replacements
  • Residential re-siding
  • Oil tank abandonment and removal
  • Woodstove or wood-burning device installation

A remodel needs a building permit application plus plans showing existing and proposed floor plans and wall details. Land use review may be needed first, and the building permit is not issued until it is approved. Electrical permits go through the state Department of Labor and Industries, at (509) 454-3700 for the Yakima office. Questions about the process go to codes@yakimawa.gov or (509) 575-6126, and applications run through buildingyakima.com.

What if my Yakima house is vacant or in poor shape?

The city responds to complaints about conditions on private property, including garbage, overgrown yards, junk vehicles and vacant buildings that are open to unauthorized entry. In March 2024 the City Council adopted the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, with local changes, as YMC Chapter 11.40.

The Code Compliance page says anyone directly affected by a notice or order can appeal to the hearing examiner, provided a written appeal is filed within 20 days after service. Reports and questions go through the Yak Back portal or the hotline at (509) 576-6657. If you inherited a vacant house and have not yet secured it, securing it early gives you more options with a buyer, whether that buyer is a family or an investor planning a rehab.

How does a deed transfer work in Yakima County?

Yakima County splits the job between two offices. According to the county's property transfer page, every transfer of real property needs a Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit processed through the County Treasurer's Office with the conveyance document. The Auditor's Recording Division then records the document. Excise tax and transfer fees must be paid in cash or certified funds.

The same order applies statewide under RCW 82.45.090, which keeps the auditor from recording a deed ahead of the tax payment or a not-due notation. Ask the Yakima County Treasurer for the amount that applies at your price, since it includes both a state and a local portion.

A mobile home follows a different path. If the sale does not require moving it, a Mobile Home Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit is used, and the Auditor's Vehicle Licensing Division handles the new owner's title. Property taxes must be paid in full before that processing. For a house, the seller also fills out the condition form from RCW 64.06.020 and gives it to the buyer shortly after contract, five business days being the default limit.

More questions about Yakima, WA

Can I sell a Yakima house with an old roof or siding?

Yes. Plenty of buyers take older roofs and siding as they are. If you decide to fix the roof or siding first, the city lets residential reroofs (tear off and reroof only) and re-siding be applied for online without plan review.

What payment form does Yakima County accept for excise tax?

Cash or certified funds. The county's property transfer page states that excise tax and transfer fees must be paid in cash or certified funds.

Can I appeal a city notice about my Yakima property?

Yes. Anyone directly affected by a property maintenance decision, notice or order may appeal to the hearing examiner. The written appeal must be filed within 20 days after the notice is served.

Where do I get an electrical permit in Yakima?

Electrical permits and inspections come from the state Department of Labor and Industries, not the city. The Yakima office is at 15 W Yakima Ave., Suite 100, and the phone number is (509) 454-3700.

Is my house in the Yakima School District?

It depends on the address. The Yakima School District runs Davis, Eisenhower, Stanton Academy and Yakima Online, while West Valley and East Valley are separate districts. Call the district office to verify the boundaries for your street.

How do you sell a house fast in Kirkland, WA?

A Kirkland owner has three routes: list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who pays without a mortgage. The cash route removes loan approval and usually the repair list, which is why it is the quickest of the three. Every route still ends at the same Washington closing items: excise tax, prorated property tax and a completed seller disclosure statement.

Kirkland is an expensive place to own a home, and that shapes the decision. The Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied housing of $1,115,400 for 2020 to 2024, with 60.8 percent of homes owner-occupied. At those values, the graduated state excise tax and the carrying cost of an empty house both matter, so a shorter timeline can be worth real money.

What is Kirkland like for a home seller?

Kirkland sits on the eastern shore of Lake Washington, and its downtown wraps around Moss Bay with restaurants, galleries, parks and a large stock of condominiums built since the 1990s. Interstate 405 links it to Bellevue, Renton and Bothell, and State Route 520 reaches Seattle and Redmond. The city covers 17.81 square miles of land and ranges from 14 to 500 feet above sea level.

The city was incorporated in 1905, merged with the neighboring town of Houghton in 1968, and grew through annexations. Totem Lake joined in 1974, South Juanita and the Rose Hill areas in 1988, and Finn Hill, North Juanita and Kingsgate on June 1, 2011, which added about 33,000 residents. A house in one of those areas can have a very different lot, age and street pattern from one near Moss Bay, so a buyer or appraiser will compare it against its own neighborhood.

  • Moss Bay and downtown: condominiums, apartments and the waterfront.
  • Houghton: where the first homesteads went up in the late 1860s.
  • Rose Hill: the hill where a steel mill was finished in 1892, with North and South Rose Hill annexed in 1988.
  • Totem Lake: annexed in 1974 and served by Sound Transit and Community Transit buses on I-405.
  • Juanita, Finn Hill and Kingsgate: the northern neighborhoods, with Finn Hill, North Juanita and Kingsgate annexed in 2011.

Most of Kirkland is in the Lake Washington School District, with Juanita High School and Lake Washington High School inside the city. Smaller parts fall in the Bellevue and Northshore districts. Evergreen Healthcare, Google and the school district were the three largest local employers in 2023.

What taxes and fees does a Kirkland seller pay at closing?

The seller normally pays Washington real estate excise tax, and it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The Department of Revenue says an unpaid tax can become a lien on the property, and interest runs if it is not paid within one month of the sale date. A local excise tax set by the city is added to the state portion, so ask your escrow officer for the combined figure on your parcel.

The state portion is graduated under RCW 82.45.060. The Department of Revenue lists these thresholds for sales beginning January 1, 2027:

  • 1.1 percent on the part of the price up to $551,000.
  • 1.28 percent on the part from $551,000 to $1,551,000.
  • 2.75 percent on the part from $1,551,000 to $3,051,000.
  • 3 percent on anything above $3,051,000.

As an illustration, a $1,200,000 sale closing in 2027 would owe $6,061 on the first slice and $8,307 on the next $649,000, about $14,368 in state tax before the local portion. Sales that close before January 1, 2027 use the earlier thresholds, which your escrow officer will apply. Details are on the Department of Revenue excise tax page.

When are King County property taxes due on a Kirkland home?

King County property tax is due in two halves, on April 30 and October 31. The second-half 2026 date has already passed, and the next first-half payment is due April 30, 2027. The King County Treasury takes payment online, by mail with a postmark on or before the due date, in person at 201 S. Jackson Street in Seattle, or at a drop box at the same building.

When a Kirkland house sells mid-year, the escrow officer prorates the bill between you and the buyer, so confirm that your last payment has posted before closing. The Treasury has posted a notice that processing of some second-half 2026 payments was delayed, and it asks owners to check the online portal to confirm their account was credited. Seniors, people with disabilities and some disabled veterans may qualify for exemption or deferral programs, which the King County Assessor administers.

Can you sell a Kirkland house that has tenants or a short-term rental license?

Yes, but Kirkland treats rentals as a business activity. The city requires a business license for any long-term or short-term rental, and operating without one can be a misdemeanor. A buyer who plans to keep the rental will ask for the license history, so have it ready.

Short-term rentals (under 30 days) fall under Ordinance O-4607, and the city's page lists the main limits for single-family homes:

  • An owner or agent who lives in the home continuously may rent short-term with no day cap, up to two rentals at a time.
  • An owner or agent present at least 245 days a year may rent short-term up to 120 days a year.
  • When no one is home, a property manager within 15 miles must be named to the city.
  • Parking is one stall per rental, plus two more stalls if permanent residents live in the home.

The city lists a $100 base fee plus a $130 per-employee regulatory fee for the business license, or $230 for many short-term rentals. Kirkland charges no business and occupation tax. A condominium is generally outside these rules, but the association's own rules still apply. Owners are responsible for lodging tax under state law.

Does Kirkland's weather affect when to sell?

Kirkland averages 36.27 inches of precipitation a year, with the wettest months being November at 5.84 inches, December at 5.43 inches and January at 4.81 inches. Summer is dry, with July averaging 0.79 inches. The record high of 109 degrees came on June 28, 2021, and snow averages 8.1 inches a year.

A winter buyer inspection happens in the wettest weather, so roof, gutter and drainage problems show up quickly. If you are fixing anything, finish those items before listing. If you are selling as-is to a cash buyer, the schedule does not depend on the season.

What must a Kirkland seller disclose?

Washington requires the seller of improved residential property to deliver a completed disclosure statement unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt, under RCW 64.06.020. The form asks about sewer or septic, roof leaks in the last five years, structural issues, and environmental concerns such as lead-based paint or storage tanks. It covers what you actually know, and the buyer has three business days from delivery to rescind unless both sides agree otherwise in writing.

Answer every line, and write NA where a question does not apply. An incomplete form invites disputes later, whether the buyer is financing or paying cash.

More questions about Kirkland, WA

How fast can a Kirkland house sell for cash?

A cash sale can close faster than a financed sale because no lender approval is required, and timing is set by title work and the closing date you choose. The county treasurer must still receive excise tax and the deed must be recorded.

Who pays the real estate excise tax in Kirkland?

The seller usually pays it, according to the Department of Revenue, and if the seller does not, the buyer becomes responsible. The tax is due to the King County treasurer on the date of sale, with interest if unpaid after one month.

Do I need a business license to rent my Kirkland house before selling?

Yes. Kirkland requires a city business license for long-term and short-term rentals, and short-term rentals also need a state license. Operating without one can be a misdemeanor, so settle that before a buyer reviews your rental records.

Are King County property taxes still due if I am selling?

Yes, until closing. Payments are due April 30 and October 31, and the escrow officer prorates the bill at closing. Check the Treasury's online portal to confirm your payment posted.

Can I sell an inherited house in Kirkland?

Yes, it can be sold once the person with legal authority to sign the deed is in place. Ask a Washington estate attorney or your title company who that is, and note that a deed transfer still goes with an excise tax affidavit to the King County treasurer.

What should you know before selling a house in Bellingham?

Selling a house in Bellingham means working in a bayfront city of 96,395 people (Census Bureau estimate for July 1, 2025) that serves as the seat of Whatcom County, roughly halfway between Seattle and Vancouver, British Columbia. Owners can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who does not need a mortgage.

The modern city dates to December 28, 1903, when four settlements on the east side of Bellingham Bay (Bellingham, Whatcom, Fairhaven and Sehome) merged. Coal mining and lumber built the early economy, and the last coal mine closed in 1955. Western Washington University, with more than 16,000 students, Whatcom Community College and Bellingham Technical College now anchor local demand for housing, and the Port of Bellingham runs the airport and the marinas.

What do the Census numbers say about Bellingham homes?

The latest Census Bureau figures show a city where renters outnumber owners and where homes carry a high price tag for Whatcom County. Those facts matter if your house has tenants, or if you expect buyers who plan to rent it out.

Which Bellingham neighborhoods and schools shape a sale?

Buyers sort Bellingham by neighborhood first. The city recognizes areas such as Alabama Hill, Barkley, Birchwood, Cordata, Cornwall Park, Edgemoor, Fairhaven, Happy Valley, the Lettered Streets, Roosevelt, Samish, Sehome, South Hill, Sunnyland, Whatcom Falls and York, along with the university district.

  • Fairhaven was platted in 1883 and has a historic commercial district whose old facades were saved by preservationists in the 1970s.
  • Sehome began around the coal mine that opened in 1854 and is part of today's downtown.
  • Cordata has a Whatcom Transportation Authority station near Bellis Fair Mall.
  • Alabama Hill is one of the higher points in town, at about 500 feet.

Most of the city belongs to the Bellingham School District, which runs four public high schools: Bellingham, Options, Sehome and Squalicum. A small northern slice of the city lies in the Meridian School District, so confirm the district for the exact address before you advertise it.

How do roads, water and weather affect a Bellingham house?

Interstate 5 splits Bellingham and links it to Seattle and Vancouver. State Route 11 runs along the Chuckanut Mountains, State Route 539 heads to Lynden and the border, and State Route 542 climbs toward Mount Baker. Whatcom Transportation Authority runs frequent Go Lines on several corridors, and Amtrak Cascades stops at Fairhaven Station twice a day.

The weather is mild. Average rainfall is 34.84 inches a year, November is the wettest month, and rain is spread over the stretch from October through April. A winter pattern called a north-Easter can send Arctic air down the Fraser River Canyon with strong wind, and a warm Pineapple Express spell can melt snow fast enough to strain drainage systems. Roofs, gutters, crawl spaces and drainage are the parts of a Bellingham house that buyers and inspectors tend to look at first.

Lake Whatcom supplies the city's drinking water and forms part of its eastern edge. That matters to sellers because Bellingham bars short-term rentals inside the Lake Whatcom watershed.

What city rules affect landlords and short-term rentals in Bellingham?

Bellingham runs a Rental Registration and Safety Inspection Program under Bellingham Municipal Code 6.15. Owners must register each rental, get a safety inspection before renting, renew the rental license every year, and have the property inspected about every three to three and a half years. Changes to the program took effect on September 7, 2026, including a required city checklist for private inspectors and a single appeal step. The city also requires 120 days of notice before a rent increase, and a rent increase of 8 percent or more triggers relocation assistance under BMC 6.14.

  • Short-term rentals fall under BMC 20.10.037 and need a land use permit.
  • In residential zones a short-term rental must be the operator's primary residence for at least 270 days a year and can be rented whole for no more than 95 days a year.
  • Short-term rentals are not allowed in the Lake Whatcom watershed or in shoreline areas.
  • Detached accessory dwelling units cannot be short-term rentals in single-family zones.

If you inherited a Bellingham house that was rented, call the Permit Center at 360-778-8300 and ask where the registration and inspection record stands before you list it.

What does a Bellingham seller owe at closing?

In Washington the seller owes real estate excise tax, and the state portion is graduated. Under RCW 82.45.060 and the Department of Revenue schedule, the current bands run from 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price to 1.28 percent up to $1,525,000, 2.75 percent up to $3,025,000 and 3 percent above that. For sales starting January 1, 2027, the department lists new break points of $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000.

As an example, a sale at the Census median value of $627,500 produces a state portion of $7,087: $5,775 on the first $525,000 plus $1,312 on the remaining $102,500. The local rate comes on top, and the county treasurer works that out for the parcel.

  • The tax is the seller's obligation under RCW 82.45.080 and is due at the time of sale.
  • Interest starts after one month, and penalties of 5, 10 and 20 percent apply at one, two and three months under RCW 82.45.100.
  • A Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit must reach the Whatcom County Treasurer, on the first floor of the courthouse at 360-778-5160, before the Auditor will record the deed.
  • The deed's first page needs a three inch top margin, grantor and grantee names, a legal description and the 16 digit assessor parcel number.

Washington also expects the seller of improved residential property to hand the buyer a completed disclosure statement within five business days after both sides sign the contract, unless the buyer waives it or an exemption applies. The buyer then has three business days to rescind (RCW 64.06.020).

When are Whatcom County property taxes due for Bellingham owners?

Whatcom County mails statements in mid-February. First-half taxes are due April 30 and second-half taxes October 31, and a bill under $50 is due in full on April 30. If the date lands on a weekend or holiday, payment is accepted the next business day. Missing the first half makes the whole year delinquent, and interest and penalty are figured on the full year, at rates set in RCW 84.56.020.

If the house is changing hands in the spring or fall, ask the closing agent how the current half will be split between you and the buyer. Whatcom County does not waive interest for a missed statement, so check the bill online even if the mail did not bring one.

What are your options for selling a Bellingham house quickly?

Three routes cover most Bellingham sellers, and the right one depends on the condition of the house, the tenants and the date you need to close.

  • List with an agent and prepare the house for showings, which suits a clean, vacant property in a sought-after neighborhood.
  • Sell it yourself, which saves the listing commission but leaves marketing, disclosure forms and negotiation to you.
  • Take a cash offer, which fits a house that needs work, a rental with an inspection problem, an inherited property or a tight deadline.

With any route, gather the last property tax statement, any rental registration paperwork, utility account details and the recorded deed. Sellers who want a direct price on a Bellingham house can request a cash offer and compare it with what a listing would net after commission, repairs and carrying costs.

More questions about Bellingham, WA

Can I sell my Bellingham house as-is?

Yes, you can sell as-is, and many Bellingham owners do. Washington still expects a completed seller disclosure statement on improved residential property unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt, so list known defects honestly.

Who pays real estate excise tax when a Bellingham house sells?

The seller pays. RCW 82.45.080 makes the tax the seller's obligation, the state portion is graduated from 1.1 percent, and the county treasurer adds the local rate when the affidavit is filed.

When are Whatcom County property taxes due?

April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. Bills under $50 are due in full on April 30, and a weekend or holiday due date moves to the next business day.

Do I need to deal with the rental program if my Bellingham house was a rental?

Yes, while the house is rented the owner has to keep the city registration current and renew it every year. Ask the Permit Center at 360-778-8300 about the status of the registration and the last safety inspection before you sell.

Can a buyer use my Bellingham house as a short-term rental?

Only with a city permit and within the zoning limits. Residential zones require the operator to live there at least 270 days a year, whole-unit rental is capped at 95 days a year, and the Lake Whatcom watershed and shoreline areas are closed to short-term rentals.

What are my options for selling a house in Kennewick?

Kennewick sellers can put the house on the market with an agent, sell it directly to another household, or accept a purchase from a buyer who pays cash. The best fit comes down to your timeline, your repair list and how much you owe.

  • Agent sale: Your house is prepared, shown and negotiated. It suits a home in good shape and an owner who can wait for the right buyer.
  • Private sale: You take on pricing, marketing and the contract. The savings come with more work.
  • Cash purchase: The buyer does not need a lender, which removes loan approval from the schedule. Compare any offer on the amount you would receive at closing.

Where is Kennewick, and how did it grow?

Kennewick sits in Benton County on the southwest bank of the Columbia River, just southeast of where the Columbia and Yakima rivers meet. It is the most populous of the three Tri-Cities, with Richland upstream on the same side and Pasco across the river. The city covers 29.962 square miles, 28.570 of them land. The 1996 discovery of Kennewick Man, a skeleton roughly 9,300 years old, is one marker of how long people have lived here.

The city was incorporated on February 5, 1904. In the 1890s a company installed pumps and ditches to bring irrigation water to the Kennewick Highlands, and orchards, vineyards and strawberries followed. The Port of Kennewick formed in 1915, the Green Bridge to Pasco opened in 1922, and the Blue Bridge followed in 1954. The Hanford site opened in 1943, and between 1940 and 1950 Kennewick grew from 1,918 residents to 10,085. Interstate 82 reached the area in 1986.

Wikipedia calls Kennewick the retail hub of the Tri-Cities, home to Columbia Center Mall, with other shopping in the historic downtown and the Southridge district. Hanford and the national laboratory still shape the economy, alongside agriculture and health care. Lamb Weston has offices in the city and Tyson Foods processes here, and Trios hospital sits in Southridge.

How do the Kennewick climate and water supply affect a house?

Kennewick has a semi-arid climate that borders on desert, because the Cascades block rain from the west. Precipitation is closer to Phoenix than to Seattle, and the mountains keep the Pacific from moderating temperatures, so extremes run higher. Winter temperature inversions in the basin can bring dense fog that lasts several days, and a 2009 dust storm obscured parts of the city in satellite images.

Flooding is part of the record. The worst Columbia River flood came in 1948, caused one death and about $50 million in damage, and led to the McNary Levee System. The flood threat from the river has fallen since the dams were built. Zintel Canyon Dam near the Southridge Sports and Events Complex protects parts of the city from a 100-year flood, but summer thunderstorms over the Horse Heaven Hills can still send flash floods down the dry creek.

Water works differently here than in many cities. The city provides drinking water and sewer, Benton Public Utility District supplies electricity, and Cascade Natural Gas provides gas. Many owners water lawns with irrigation water from nearby rivers, delivered separately by the Kennewick Irrigation District, or the Columbia Irrigation District on parts of the east side. Ask the district that serves your address for any assessment balance before closing.

What do I pay and file with Benton County when I sell?

The Benton County Treasurer collects property tax for the county, the cities, school districts, fire departments and other taxing districts, based on valuations set by the Assessor. The Kennewick office is at 7122 W Okanogan Pl, Suite E110, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and reachable at 509-735-8505. The treasurer's page currently lists an office closure for Thanksgiving, so plan a late-November closing around it.

  • Property tax: Under RCW 84.56.020, when the total is $50 or more, half is due by April 30 and the second half by October 31. A payment is delinquent after those dates.
  • Excise tax: The seller usually pays Washington's real estate excise tax. At the median value of $370,700, state tax at 1.1 percent comes to about $4,078, since the price stays within the first $525,000 bracket.
  • Forms: The treasurer's forms page lists the Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit, a supplemental statement and a refund request.

The Department of Revenue states that excise tax is due to the county treasurer on the sale date, with penalty and interest if unpaid after one month. Your escrow officer will normally prepare the affidavit.

Which projects need a permit in Kennewick?

Some do not, which helps if you are fixing small things before a sale. Kennewick's Building Safety Division lists exceptions to building permits: detached residential accessory structures up to 200 square feet that meet setbacks and stay off easements, retaining walls up to 4 feet high, finish work such as painting, tiling, carpeting and cabinets, prefabricated pools under 24 inches deep, and window awnings that project no more than 54 inches.

New single-family residences of up to two units skip a land use permit, but they still need a building permit. For any question, call Building Safety at 509-585-4276 or Community Planning at 509-585-4280.

How do roads, schools and transit shape buyer interest in Kennewick?

Interstate 82 bypasses the city to the south and links to Seattle by way of I-90 and to Portland by way of I-84. U.S. 395 runs north to south, State Route 240 crosses the Blue Bridge to Pasco, and State Route 397 crosses the Cable Bridge. Ben Franklin Transit runs routes through two transit centers, Three Rivers near the Toyota Center and Dayton Transfer Point downtown. The nearest commercial airport is the Tri-Cities Airport in Pasco, whose busiest route goes to Seattle-Tacoma.

Kennewick School District operates 17 elementary schools, five middle schools and three high schools, and serves over 18,000 students. The Tri-Tech Skills Center offers programs such as firefighting, radio broadcasting and auto body technology.

What should I confirm before accepting an offer on my Kennewick house?

  • Get the price, the closing date and every cost assigned to you in writing.
  • Request a payoff statement from your lender, then subtract it, the excise tax and any irrigation district balance to see your real proceeds.
  • Ask the buyer to explain how the purchase will be funded and what, if anything, depends on an inspection.
  • Check with Building Safety about any shed, addition or remodel you are unsure was permitted.
  • Ask the Benton County Treasurer for the current tax status on your parcel.

More questions about Kennewick, WA

Which county is Kennewick in, and where do I pay property tax?

Benton County. The Benton County Treasurer collects property tax for the county, the city and school districts. The Kennewick office is at 7122 W Okanogan Pl, Suite E110, and the phone number is 509-735-8505.

One-half is due by April 30 and the remainder by October 31, according to RCW 84.56.020. Payments after those dates are delinquent and carry interest and penalties. Ask the treasurer for a current statement on your parcel.

Do I need a permit to put up a shed in Kennewick?

Not always. A detached residential accessory structure up to 200 square feet is exempt from a building permit if it meets setbacks and stays off easements. Larger sheds need a building permit. Call Building Safety at 509-585-4276.

Which school district serves Kennewick?

The Kennewick School District serves the city's public schools, with 17 elementary schools, five middle schools and three high schools. It serves over 18,000 students and helps fund the Tri-Tech Skills Center.

Does the Columbia River still flood Kennewick?

The risk from the river has dropped since the dams and the McNary Levee System were built, after the 1948 flood. Flash floods from the Horse Heaven Hills can still occur in Zintel Canyon during summer thunderstorms. Ask the city for the status of your parcel.

What should I know before selling a house in Auburn, WA?

Auburn is a King County city of 86,301 people (Census Bureau estimate for July 1, 2025) with a small piece that crosses into Pierce County, so the county that bills your property tax depends on which side of the line the house sits. Auburn leans toward ownership: 60.6% of housing is owner-occupied, the median value of an owner-occupied home was $547,900 for 2020 to 2024, and the typical household has 2.79 people. Median household income was $97,884 and the average commute was 30.5 minutes.

The 2025 estimate sits below the 87,256 counted in the 2020 census, which itself was well above the 70,180 counted in 2010. A good share of that earlier jump came from annexation. In 2008 Auburn annexed the West Hill and Lea Hill areas of unincorporated King County, which added about 15,000 residents, and on January 1, 2024 it took in the 155-acre Bridges neighborhood from Kent.

That history explains why an "Auburn" mailing address does not always mean the City of Auburn. Some addresses that include Auburn belong to King County, Kent or Federal Way, and the city's permit page asks you to check its interactive map before assuming city rules apply to your property.

How did Auburn grow, and which neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

The town was platted in 1886 as Slaughter, named for an officer killed in 1855, and incorporated on June 13, 1891. The legislature changed the name to Auburn on February 21, 1893, after Auburn, New York, where residents shared a hops-farming economy. Floods on the White and Green rivers shaped the early valley until Mud Mountain Dam and Howard A. Hanson Dam were completed, which let the city grow without that constraint.

The largest recent build-out was Lakeland Hills. Construction began in 1985 on a master-planned community in the hills southeast of downtown, and by 2007 it had 3,600 homes and about 6,000 residents. Auburn voted in 1997 to annex part of it, and the city finished taking in the Pierce County portion by the end of that decade.

  • Downtown: historic buildings, a traditional main street and Craftsman-style houses from the 1920s.
  • Lea Hill: mostly residential, east of the valley, and home to Green River College.
  • Lakeland Hills: master-planned and split between King and Pierce counties.
  • Terminal Park: middle-class housing near the rail yard, named for railroad workers.
  • Forest Villa: residential, around Game Farm Park.
  • West Hill: borders Federal Way.
  • Hidden Valley: planned development east of Lakeland Hills overlooking North Lake Tapps.

Which school districts serve Auburn homes?

Most of the city is in the Auburn School District, which is larger than the city itself and also serves Algona, Pacific and some unincorporated areas. Parts of north Auburn are served by the Federal Way and Kent school districts, and the Pierce County portion falls in the Dieringer School District. Because the boundary depends on the street, confirm the district for your exact address before you list.

The public high schools are Auburn High School, Auburn Mountainview High School and Auburn Riverside High School. Private options include Auburn Adventist Academy, Rainier Christian High School, Valley Christian School and Holy Family School, and Green River College is on Lea Hill. The Auburn School District, with 2,536 employees, is the city's second largest employer.

How do jobs, roads and weather affect Auburn houses?

Auburn's economy leans on aerospace, distribution and health care. The Boeing plant, opened in 1966, is the largest airplane parts plant in the world. The city's 2022 annual financial report lists the biggest employers.

  • The Boeing Company: 3,600 employees.
  • Auburn School District: 2,536.

For commuters, State Route 167 (the Valley Freeway) and State Route 18 run through town. Auburn station is a hub for the Green River Valley: Sounder trains reach downtown Seattle in about 30 minutes, Sound Transit buses connect to Federal Way, Sumner and Kent, and King County Metro buses serve Auburn Way and Green River College.

The climate is mild and wet. Average precipitation is 37.1 inches a year, with the heaviest months being November (6.1 inches), December (5.8) and January (5.3). Summers are dry, with July and August highs near 77 and 78 degrees, and the record high is 100.

Do I need a rental license in Auburn?

Yes for most rentals. Auburn requires an owner to obtain a Rental Housing License for most forms of renting residential property, and the program exists so the city has current ownership and management information for non-owner-occupied homes. If you are selling a house that tenants occupy, confirm your license is current before you list. The city lists the following arrangements.

What permits and disclosures come up when selling an Auburn house?

Auburn takes permit applications electronically through MyBuildingPermit.com. Electrical permits inside city limits come from the Washington Department of Labor and Industries, and a house on a septic system needs approval from the King County or Pierce County health department for most changes. If you built a deck, finished a basement or changed wiring, find out now whether a permit exists, because buyers and inspectors ask.

State law also puts a form in your hands. Under RCW 64.06.020, the seller of improved residential property delivers a completed disclosure statement, unless the buyer waived it or the transfer is exempt, no later than five business days after mutual acceptance of a written contract. The buyer then has three business days after delivery to rescind. The form begins with questions about title and water and goes on from there, so start gathering records before you list.

How are property tax and transfer tax handled when selling in Auburn?

A King County parcel is billed by the King County treasurer and a Pierce County parcel by the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer, whose office can be reached at (253) 798-6111. Under RCW 84.56.020, the first half is due April 30 and the second half October 31. Taxes are a lien from January 1, and RCW 84.60.020 splits the year between seller and buyer by days when the contract is silent. Escrow normally prorates the bill at closing.

The seller usually pays the state real estate excise tax, due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the first $551,000 of price is taxed at 1.1%, with 1.28% from $551,000 to $1,551,000 and higher rates above that. Auburn's Census median value of $547,900 sits just below the first bracket, so a typical sale there would be taxed entirely at the lowest state rate, plus the local share. Ask your closing agent to confirm the local rate and any exemption you may claim.

Washington lets residents 61 or older, certain disabled owners and some veterans claim a property tax exemption under RCW 84.36.381, and the status can move to a replacement home if you sell.

Which county do I pay property tax to if I live in Auburn?

Most Auburn parcels are in King County and are billed by the King County treasurer. Homes in the Pierce County portion, including part of Lakeland Hills, are billed by the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer.

Does my Auburn mailing address mean I am inside Auburn city limits?

Not always. Some addresses that include Auburn fall under King County, Kent or Federal Way, so use the city's interactive map before assuming city permit and rental rules apply.

Do I need a city license to rent rooms in my Auburn home?

You need a City of Auburn business license if you rent rooms to more than two people. Renting to two or fewer people in an owner-occupied home does not require one, and the occupancy limit is family plus 2.

How soon must I give the buyer a seller disclosure statement?

Deliver it no later than five business days after the buyer and seller mutually accept a written contract, unless the buyer waived it or the transfer is exempt. The buyer then has three business days to rescind.

For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state rate is 1.1% on the portion of the price up to $551,000, so a sale at Auburn's $547,900 median value would fall in that bracket. A local rate is added.

What should a seller know about Pasco, Washington?

Pasco is the county seat of Franklin County and one of the three Tri-Cities, with Kennewick and Richland across the Columbia River to the south. The Census Bureau estimates 82,848 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 7.1% from the April 2020 estimates base.

Pasco was incorporated on September 3, 1891, as a Northern Pacific Railway town. Grand Coulee Dam, completed in 1941, brought irrigation to the area and tied the city to farming for decades. The city covers about 34 square miles, roughly 30.5 of them land.

A seller here deals with city hall for permits and rental licenses, with the Franklin County Treasurer for tax and excise payments, and with the Pasco School District for school boundaries that buyers ask about. The rest of this page covers each in turn.

What do the Census numbers say about Pasco homes?

Seven in ten Pasco homes are owner-occupied. The table shows the main figures from Census QuickFacts.

MeasurePasco city

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts. Households average 3.19 people, and the Census reports that 53.0% of residents age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home. If you or your buyer want signing help in another language, ask the closing office to arrange it early.

How does Pasco's desert climate affect a house sale?

Pasco sits in the rain shadow of the Cascade Range, so the area is dry and windy. Summers are hot, with a mean daily high of 93.3 degrees in July and a record high of 115 degrees in June, and winters are cold enough to reach a record low of minus 19 degrees in January.

Those swings put a premium on a few items a buyer will check:

  • Air conditioning age and capacity, since cooling runs for months.
  • Roof condition and attic insulation under strong summer sun.
  • Irrigation systems and landscaping that survive on little rain.
  • Pipes and exterior faucets that can freeze in a cold snap.

Service records for the cooling system and roof give a buyer something concrete to review. If a unit is near the end of its life, say so on the disclosure form rather than waiting for the inspector.

What do Pasco schools, jobs and neighborhoods mean for a seller?

The Pasco School District runs the city's public schools. Pasco High School is the older of two long-standing high schools, Chiawana High School opened in August 2009, and a third, Sageview High School, opened in 2025 to relieve crowding at Chiawana. Delta High School, a STEM program shared with the Kennewick and Richland districts, opened in 2015. Columbia Basin College and Washington State University Tri-Cities serve the city's students.

The Census shows 67.0% of residents age 16 and older in the labor force, and Census business data show about $359 million in 2022 transportation and warehousing receipts in Pasco. Mean travel time to work is 22.5 minutes. Buyers who commute across the river to Kennewick or Richland will weigh that against price.

Parts of Pasco are newer subdivisions and parts are older neighborhoods near downtown, so a nearby sale of a similar house is a better guide to price than the citywide median. Ask an agent or your cash buyer which recent sales they used.

Which Pasco city rules matter before you sell?

Pasco's Ordinance No. 4770, adopted June 2, 2025, removed permit requirements for several small jobs. The city's permit page lists them, and they matter if you want to tidy the house before listing:

  • One-story detached sheds or playhouses up to 200 square feet in residential areas.
  • Fences under 7 feet, retaining walls under 4 feet, and decks under 200 square feet and 30 inches high.
  • Residential roofing and siding replacement limited to the shingles, underlayment, flashing, siding, barrier and veneer.

Structural work, anything habitable, and building in an easement or too close to a property line still need a permit. A permit is good for 180 days from issue, and passing an inspection renews that clock, according to the city's ADU guide.

That guide, published in 2023, says Pasco allows one attached or detached ADU per residential parcel, up to 1,000 square feet or 55 percent of the main house, whichever is less. The unit must be long-term housing, with occupants living there more than 180 days a year, and short-term rentals are not allowed. Landlords need a rental business license under PMC 5.60.010. Call Pasco Community and Economic Development at (509) 545-3441 to confirm current rules for your zone.

How is real estate excise tax handled on a Pasco sale?

The seller owes it. RCW 82.45.080 makes the excise tax the seller's obligation. The state portion is 1.1% on the part of the price up to $525,000, then 1.28% to $1,525,000, then 2.75% to $3,025,000 and 3% above that, with the local portion added on top.

At the Census median of $376,300, the state portion alone would be about $4,139. The Department of Revenue moves the thresholds to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000 for sales beginning January 1, 2027. Ask the Franklin County Treasurer for the local rate.

Payment is due on the date of sale, which is the date the deed is notarized, and the one-month grace period before interest starts runs from that date. You submit the affidavit, the deed and the payment to the county treasurer. If a seller overpays, a refund request must be filed within four years of the sale and the refund goes to the party who paid. The Department of Revenue REET page has the forms.

How do Franklin County property taxes work at closing?

Franklin County's Treasurer says taxes are payable on or after February 15, with the full amount due by April 30. When the bill is more than $50, half can be paid by April 30 and the second half by October 31. The Treasurer is at 1016 N 4th Avenue in Pasco, phone 509-545-3518.

For real property, the Treasurer starts foreclosure action when taxes have been delinquent for three years, so a seller with old arrears should pay them off at closing. Ask your closing officer for a current tax status before you sign.

Owners who are 61 or older, disabled, or disabled veterans may qualify for a deduction, and the Franklin County Assessor handles those applications at 509-545-3506. If you are selling because you can no longer keep up with the house, ask the Assessor whether a reduction would have applied in a prior year.

What options does a Pasco seller have?

A seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept an as-is offer from a cash buyer. Each ends with the same deed, affidavit and tax steps, so the choice comes down to timing, condition and price.

  • A listing suits a house in good shape and an owner who can wait through showings and financing.
  • A direct as-is sale suits a house with deferred repairs, a tenant, or an inherited property.
  • Ask any buyer who pays the excise tax, how the date of sale is set, and how back taxes are handled.

More questions about Pasco, WA

How much is the excise tax on a Pasco house sale?

It is 1.1% on the first $525,000 of the price under current state rules, plus a local portion set for Pasco. A $376,300 sale would owe about $4,139 at the state rate. The Franklin County Treasurer can quote the local rate.

When are Franklin County property taxes due?

The full tax is due by April 30, and for bills over $50 you may pay half by April 30 and the second half by October 31. The October 31, 2026 date has passed, so the next deadline is April 30, 2027.

Can I rent out an ADU in Pasco as a vacation rental?

No. The city's ADU guide says an ADU must be used for long-term residential purposes, with occupants living there more than 180 days a year, and short-term rentals are not allowed.

Do I need a permit to replace my roof in Pasco?

Not for a shingle, underlayment and flashing replacement. Ordinance 4770 removed that requirement, but structural roof work still needs a permit.

Who do I call about taxes for a senior or disabled owner in Franklin County?

The Franklin County Assessor at 509-545-3506. The county lists a deduction for owners who are 61 or older, disabled, or disabled veterans.

How can I sell my house fast in Redmond, WA?

You can sell a Redmond house quickly by accepting a cash offer, listing it with an agent, or selling it yourself. The right route depends on how much time you have, what shape the house is in, and how much you want to spend before closing.

Redmond is a King County city about 15 miles east of Seattle, and the Census Bureau puts its July 2025 population at 82,506. Demand here is tied closely to the tech payroll around the Microsoft campus, so a house near the Overlake or downtown light rail stations often draws a different buyer pool than one on Education Hill or in the outer residential streets. Before you choose a route, decide which of these matters most:

  • A firm closing date, for example because of a move, a job change or a probate deadline.
  • The highest possible price, which usually means repairs, staging and a few weeks of showings.
  • Selling the house exactly as it stands, with the furniture, the deferred maintenance and any unpermitted work.

A cash buyer purchases without waiting on a lender, so the timeline depends mostly on title work and your own schedule. Ask any buyer to put the price, the closing date, who pays closing costs and any credits for repairs in writing so you can compare offers side by side.

What should a Redmond seller know about the city itself?

Redmond sits on the north end of Lake Sammamish, with the downtown core just north of the lake and the Sammamish River running along the west edge of downtown. The city was incorporated on December 31, 1912, and grew from about 11,000 residents in 1970 to 73,256 in the 2020 census. Its borders touch Kirkland to the west, Bellevue to the southwest and Sammamish to the southeast.

Neighborhoods matter to buyers, and a few stand out. Overlake lies southwest of downtown and holds the Microsoft headquarters campus plus apartments and houses. Education Hill sits north of downtown and takes its name from the five schools built there. Newer growth has gone into the downtown and Overlake areas, where the 2 Line light rail now serves the city: the first section opened in April 2024 and the extension to Downtown Redmond opened on May 10, 2025.

Schools shape which families look at a given street. Most of Redmond belongs to the Lake Washington School District, which runs Redmond High School and Nikola Tesla STEM High School. The Bellevue School District covers the southernmost neighborhoods, mainly below NE 40th Street, and the unincorporated English Hill area is in the Northshore School District. When you list or negotiate, name the district for your address, since buyers search by it.

The local economy is dominated by Microsoft, which reported 44,782 employees in Redmond in the city's 2021 financial report, with Meta, Nintendo of America and the Lake Washington School District also among the largest employers. A 2023 figure cited for the city is that about 89 percent of employees of Redmond companies commute in from elsewhere, which keeps interest in nearby housing steady.

How do Redmond housing numbers compare with nearby cities?

Redmond homes are among the higher-priced in the state, and a large share of residents rent. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts figures below put Redmond next to two neighbors in the same county.

Measure (Census Bureau QuickFacts)RedmondRentonSammamish
Population estimate, July 1, 202582,506104,97566,110
Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024$1,167,800$672,600$1,407,300
Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 202443.2%54.4%82.6%
Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024$2,409$1,998$2,857

The owner-occupied rate of 43.2 percent means more than half of Redmond households rent. That is why many sellers here are former landlords or heirs who inherited a rental, and why the rental and short-term rental rules below are worth reading before you decide.

Does Redmond weather affect how a house sells?

Yes, because buyers and inspectors look for water and heat damage. Redmond has a mild climate with cool, wet winters. Average precipitation peaks in December at 5.45 inches and November is the rainiest month, so roof condition, gutters, crawl spaces and drainage tend to come up in inspections. Snow is uncommon, and the record high is 111 degrees Fahrenheit, set on June 28, 2021.

Washington's seller disclosure form asks directly about these points. Plan to answer questions such as:

  • Has the roof leaked in the last five years?
  • Has the basement flooded or leaked, or has there been standing water or a drainage problem?
  • Were building permits and final inspections obtained for any additions, conversions or remodeling?
  • Are there critical areas, wetlands or floodplains on the property?

Under RCW 64.06.020 the completed form must reach the buyer within five business days after both sides accept a written contract, unless otherwise agreed, and the buyer then has three business days after delivery to rescind unless the right was waived. The statute also says the seller must provide at least one smoke detection device and equip the home with carbon monoxide alarms as the state building code requires.

Do Redmond permits and rental rules matter when I sell?

They can, especially if you added space or have rented the house. Redmond requires a building permit for additions, remodels, garage conversions, decks and accessory dwelling units. Work that needs no permit includes one-story detached accessory structures up to 200 square feet, retaining walls not over 4 feet, and replacing windows in the existing openings. New homes and detached accessory dwelling units must have fire sprinklers, according to the city's residential permits page.

If past work was done without a permit, tell the buyer on the disclosure form. A cash purchase as-is lets you transfer the house without finishing that paperwork, although the buyer will price the risk in. The Development Services counter can tell you what the file shows for your address.

Short-term rentals changed recently. Redmond adopted Ordinance 3239 on December 2, 2025, and a City of Redmond business license for short-term rentals took effect on January 1, 2026, in addition to the state license. The city issues one license per individually addressed rental in single-family areas and one per operator in multifamily or mixed-use buildings. Rentals under 30 consecutive nights are the ones covered, and an owner-occupied home with fewer than three rooms rented for at least six months a year falls outside the definition. Operating without a license carries a penalty equal to 100 percent of the fee, so confirm your standing before you hand over an operating rental.

What taxes and paperwork come with closing a Redmond sale?

The seller usually pays the Washington real estate excise tax, and it is due to the county treasurer where the property sits on the date of sale. The Department of Revenue treats the date the deed is notarized as the date of sale. A graduated state rate applies to the selling price, and a local rate is added on top. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state brackets are:

  • 1.1% on the portion up to $551,000
  • 1.28% on the portion above $551,000 up to $1,551,000
  • 2.75% on the portion above $1,551,000 up to $3,051,000
  • 3.0% on the portion above $3,051,000

Ask your escrow officer or the King County Recorder's Office for the local rate and the amount for a Redmond address, and for the thresholds that apply to a sale that closes before the new year. If the tax is not paid within one month of the sale, interest starts running, and the Department of Revenue lists an assessment rate of 6 percent for 2026.

Property tax is separate. Under RCW 84.56.020 taxes are due April 30, and half can be paid then with the rest by October 31 when the total is $50 or more. Taxes follow the parcel, so closing should prorate the current year between you and the buyer. Request a tax statement from King County Treasury before you accept a closing date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Redmond houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do listing, selling yourself and a cash sale compare?

Each route trades price against speed and certainty. The points below are the ones Redmond sellers weigh most often.

  • Listing with an agent: widest exposure to Eastside buyers, with showings, inspections and repair negotiations before closing.
  • Selling on your own: you keep the commission amount but handle the marketing, the disclosure form, the contract and the excise tax affidavit yourself.
  • Cash sale as-is: fewer steps and a closing date you pick, with an offer that reflects the house's condition.

Whichever you choose, gather the same documents first: the deed, any loan payoff statement, permit records, HOA documents if the home is in an association, and your latest property tax statement. Having them ready shortens every route.

More questions about Redmond, WA

How long does it take to sell a house in Redmond, WA for cash?

It varies by buyer and by title work, so ask for the closing date in writing. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which usually shortens the timeline compared with a financed listing. Your own deadlines, such as a payoff or probate step, still set the pace.

Who pays the real estate excise tax when I sell in Redmond?

The seller usually pays, according to the Washington Department of Revenue, and the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. If the seller does not pay, the buyer becomes responsible and the tax can become a lien on the property. Your escrow officer will calculate the state and local amounts.

Do I have to give the buyer a disclosure form in Redmond?

Yes, for most sales of improved residential property, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt under RCW 64.06.010. The form is due within five business days after a written contract is accepted, and the buyer has three business days after delivery to rescind.

Can I sell a Redmond house that has unpermitted work?

Yes, but you should disclose it. The state form asks whether permits and final inspections were obtained for additions and remodeling. A buyer who purchases as-is will account for the issue in the price. Contact Redmond Development Services to see which permits are on file.

Do I need a business license to sell a Redmond house that was a short-term rental?

A license is needed to operate a short-term rental, not to sell the house. Since January 1, 2026, Redmond requires a city business license for qualifying short-term rentals. If the rental ran without one, resolve any penalty questions with the city's finance office before closing.

What are your options for a fast house sale in Marysville, WA?

Marysville owners generally choose among listing with an agent, selling directly to a buyer they find themselves, or taking a cash purchase on the house as it stands. Time is the main variable. A listing needs prep, showings and a financed buyer's loan approval, while a cash sale can compress the schedule when the house has deferred maintenance, a tenant, or a pending deadline.

Marysville is now the second-largest city in Snohomish County, with a Census Bureau estimate of 77,686 residents in July 2025, up 9.9 percent from the April 2020 estimates base.

Whatever route you pick, collect these documents first.

  • The deed and your most recent Snohomish County property tax statement.
  • Payoff letters from your lender and any lienholder.
  • Receipts and permit records for major work, such as a roof, addition or deck.
  • Your completed seller disclosure statement.

What does the Census say about Marysville homes and households?

Marysville is mostly an owner-occupied city with prices below Lynnwood and well above Longview. These figures come from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts for the city.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 69.4 percent.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $567,900.
  • Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage: $2,409.
  • Median gross rent: $1,997.
  • Households: 25,969, averaging 2.79 persons.
  • Median household income: $103,974.
  • Mean travel time to work: 31.5 minutes.

Those numbers describe the whole city, so treat them as background. Your own price depends on the house, its condition and recent sales on your block.

How did Marysville grow, and what does the land look like?

James and Maria Comeford started a trading post here in 1872 on the edge of the Tulalip Indian Reservation. The town was platted on February 25, 1885, and incorporated as a fourth-class city on March 20, 1891, the same year the Great Northern Railway came through. Strawberry fields covered more than 2,000 acres by 1920, which gave Marysville its nickname, Strawberry City, and the Strawberry Festival has been held since 1932.

Growth came in waves. Suburban development began in the 1970s and 1980s, the population grew fivefold between 1980 and 2000, and annexations to the north and east in the early 2000s pushed the city past 20 square miles and 60,000 residents. Marysville runs north to south along Interstate 5, with the Tulalip reservation to the west and State Route 9 to the east.

The terrain matters when you sell. Downtown sits about 5 feet above sea level along Ebey Slough, while the land climbs to about 160 feet near Smokey Point and over 465 feet in the eastern highlands. Two creeks, Quilceda and Allen, drain the area along with roughly 70 smaller streams. If your house is low or near water, ask the county for the flood zone information and a survey so a buyer's lender does not raise it first.

How do commutes and roads affect a Marysville listing?

Most Marysville workers commute out of the city. About 9 percent of residents work inside city limits, roughly 20 percent work in Everett and 13 percent in Seattle, and the average one-way trip is around 32 minutes, with 70 percent driving alone. The Census Bureau lists mean travel time at 31.5 minutes.

Community Transit runs four local bus routes in Marysville and express service from park and ride lots, including all-day service to Lynnwood City Center station and peak service to the Boeing Everett Factory. Marysville sits outside the Sound Transit service area. The state began work in 2023 on a northbound high-occupancy vehicle lane on I-5 and a new interchange at State Route 529, and in 2014 voters approved a 0.2 percent sales tax for city transportation improvements.

Buyers weigh access to I-5 and State Route 529 heavily, so state in plain terms how long your house is from the on-ramp and from Everett.

Which school district serves Marysville?

The Marysville School District covers most of the incorporated city and the Tulalip Indian Reservation, and its high schools are Marysville Pilchuck and Marysville Getchell. Parts of the city fall in the Arlington, Lake Stevens or Lakewood school districts, so a buyer with children will want to confirm the district for your exact address.

What do Marysville permits cost in time, and what rules affect an ADU?

Residential permit typeAverage review, days (Q1 2026)

Building permit applications go through the city's online permit portal. Permit questions can go to MSVLPermits@marysvillewa.gov, and planning questions to Planning@marysvillewa.gov. The phone line, 360-363-8000, is staffed from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Accessory dwelling units are a selling point on larger lots. Marysville's ADU guide says a lot may have two ADUs, each between 200 square feet and the greater of 1,000 square feet or 50 percent of the main house, capped at 1,400 square feet, with one parking space per unit and separate water and sewer connections in most cases. The same guide states that short-term rental units are prohibited in the city, so do not market a house or ADU to a buyer as a short-term rental.

To find your zoning, the city publishes a zoning map. For property lines, the city says a licensed survey is the only reliable answer, and recorded surveys can be searched through the Snohomish County Auditor.

What does Washington law require when you sell in Marysville?

Two state rules shape most Marysville closings. First, RCW 64.06.020 requires the seller disclosure statement within five business days of mutual acceptance unless the parties agree otherwise, and the buyer can rescind within three business days after receiving it. Second, the real estate excise tax is due when the sale occurs, usually from the seller.

The Department of Revenue's graduated state rate for sales starting January 1, 2027 is 1.1 percent through $551,000, 1.28 percent through $1,551,000, 2.75 percent through $3,051,000 and 3 percent beyond. Earlier sales use $525,000, $1,525,000 and $3,025,000 as the breakpoints. A local rate is added, so ask the Snohomish County Treasurer for the combined figure on your price. With a city median value of $567,900, a typical Marysville sale crosses into the 1.28 percent band.

How does Snohomish County value and tax a Marysville house?

Snohomish County's assessor must appraise real property at 100 percent of true and fair market value, using a sales comparison, a replacement cost, or an income approach. The county revalues every year as of January 1 and mails the notice in June. The value in that notice is used to calculate the next year's tax.

If you think the number is off, call the assessor's phone number on the notice and ask for an appraiser. The next step is a Board of Equalization petition, which must be filed within 60 days of the mailing or by July 1, whichever is later, and the clerk can be reached at 425-388-3407. The two tax installments are due April 30 and October 31, and a mailed payment must be postmarked by then. Your escrow company will prorate the current bill at closing.

How do you judge a cash offer on a Marysville house?

Judge it by what you keep after all costs. Add up the offer, subtract the payoff and excise tax, and compare the result with the list-price scenario after commission, repair credits and the months of payments you would carry. Ask for the closing date in writing, and have a title company handle the transfer.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

More questions about Marysville, WA

How long does a Marysville permit take to review?

It depends on the type. The city's Q1 2026 averages were 8 days for decks, 18 for remodels, 26 for new residential and 34 for accessory dwelling units, counted in calendar days of staff review. Your project may take longer if the city asks for revisions.

Can I use a Marysville ADU as a short-term rental?

No. The city's ADU standards guide says short-term rental units are currently prohibited in Marysville. A buyer who plans nightly rentals would need to look at other options.

What is the deadline to appeal my Snohomish County assessed value?

You must file a completed petition with the Board of Equalization within 60 days of the notice mailing or by July 1, whichever is later. The clerk of the board is at 425-388-3407. You do not need an attorney, but you do need evidence that the value is wrong.

Who pays the Washington excise tax on a house sale?

Usually the seller. The Department of Revenue says the buyer is responsible if the seller does not pay. The tax goes to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and your closing agent normally deducts it from your proceeds.

Do I have to give a Marysville buyer a disclosure statement?

In most sales of improved residential property, yes. RCW 64.06.020 sets the form and the five business day delivery window, and the buyer can rescind within three business days after receiving it. A buyer can waive the right in writing, and some transfers are exempt.

What is it like to sell a house in Shoreline?

Shoreline is a mostly owner-occupied suburb just north of Seattle. The Census Bureau estimates 66,542 residents as of July 1, 2025, a rise of 13.8 percent from the 2020 base. About 66.3 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and 88.3 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, against 78.1 percent in Seattle.

The city sits in the northwest corner of King County, immediately north of Seattle at North 145th Street and south of Snohomish County along North 205th Street. Puget Sound forms the western edge, and Lake Forest Park lies to the east. Shoreline incorporated on August 31, 1995.
