How did Shoreline develop, and why does it matter to a seller?

Shoreline grew from a railroad plat and a school district. Richmond Beach was platted in 1890 in anticipation of the Great Northern Railway. The Seattle to Everett Interurban streetcar arrived in 1906, and North Trunk Road, now Aurora Avenue North (State Route 99), followed in 1913.

The name came in 1944, when the school district took it to describe boundaries that ran from shore to shore and from the old Seattle city limit at 85th Street to the Snohomish County line. From 1950 to 1957 the area grew faster than any other part of the Seattle region, with a 64 percent population increase. Seattle began studying annexation in 1988, which pushed residents to organize the incorporation vote that created the city in 1995.

The city is divided into 14 neighborhoods, with Richmond Beach in the northwest corner. It also contains The Highlands, a gated community designed by the Olmsted Brothers that has its own sewer district. If your house is in a neighborhood with unusual rules or a homeowners' association, say so early, because the state disclosure form asks about association assessments, common areas and approvals for remodeling.

Do I need permits for work on a Shoreline house before selling?

Often yes, and the city treats missing permits as a violation that follows the property. Shoreline's permit FAQ says failure to get a permit before construction starts breaks city code and can bring fines and penalties, and permit fees may be doubled. The same page states that property owners are responsible for work earlier owners did without permits. That makes a pre-sale check worthwhile.

These points come straight from the city's guidance:

  • Simple interior work such as replacing cabinets, painting and tiling generally does not need a permit unless it involves plumbing, electrical or gas work.
  • Moving walls, doors or windows likely requires a building permit, and so does replacing a water heater or adding a permanently wired light fixture.
  • Some trades permits, such as plumbing or mechanical, can be issued the same day. Other review times vary by project type and the quality of the documents.
  • Applications go through the city's eTRAKiT system, and you can view a permit's status without an account. Questions can go to pcd@shorelinewa.gov.
  • Work that began without a permit can require a separate investigation inspection permit before the building permit is submitted.

Trees need a check too. A tree that is an imminent hazard can be removed under the municipal code, but a healthy tree with only moderate risk may still require a permit. Removing a tree without one can bring penalties sometimes reaching $15,000 or more.

  • Water: Seattle Public Utilities or North City Water District, depending on the address. The city's property information map shows the service area.
  • Garbage, recycling and compost: Recology.
  • Natural gas: Puget Sound Energy.

The city manages wastewater everywhere except The Highlands. Two treatment facilities serve the city, one run by Edmonds and one by King County, and a map layer on the city's managed assets viewer shows which one a parcel drains to. The seller disclosure form asks whether the property is on a public sewer, whether the house is connected, and whether extra sewer charges apply, so confirm those answers with the city before you sign.

Which schools, roads and light rail stations serve Shoreline?

The Shoreline School District serves the city, with Shorecrest High School and Shorewood High School as its two high schools. A third, Shoreline High School, closed in June 1986, and its 1,000 students were split between the other two. Shoreline Community College is in the city, and the former Shoreline High campus became the district headquarters and the Spartan Campus, with a public gym, theater and stadium.

Interstate 5 and State Route 99 (Aurora Avenue) run north to south through the city, and State Route 523 (145th Street) forms the southern boundary. Two Link light rail stations sit beside Interstate 5: Shoreline South/148th and Shoreline North/185th, with park-and-ride garages holding a combined 1,000 stalls. King County Metro runs the RapidRide E Line on Aurora, and the Interurban Trail follows State Route 99 and was finished within the city in September 2007.

Shoreline works as a bedroom community. Census data shows 46.7 percent of resident workers commute to Seattle and only 7.3 percent work inside Shoreline, while the mean commute is 27.2 minutes. Costco, Fred Meyer and Home Depot are among the largest employers, along with the city, the school district and the state transportation department, mostly along Aurora.

What does a Shoreline seller pay at closing?

The largest item is the state real estate excise tax, which the seller normally pays. If the seller does not, the buyer owes it and the unpaid amount can become a lien. It is a graduated tax: 1.1 percent on the portion of the price up to $525,000, 1.28 percent from there to $1,525,000, then 2.75 percent and 3 percent in higher bands. Sales beginning January 1, 2027 use break points of $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000.

As an illustration, a sale at the $811,100 Census median value that closes before 2027 would owe about $9,437 in state tax: $5,775 on the first $525,000 and $3,662 on the remaining $286,100. A local rate is added on top. Ask the King County treasurer for the Shoreline rate and for your parcel's property tax balance, and ask your escrow officer how the current year's bill will be handled.

The seller disclosure statement must be delivered within five business days after the buyer and seller accept a written contract, and the buyer can rescind within three business days of delivery unless the right was waived. The form also tells the seller to confirm that carbon monoxide alarms and smoke detection are in place.

The Census Bureau estimates 66,542 residents as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 58,608, so the city has grown about 13.8 percent from the 2020 base.

Do I need a permit to remodel a Shoreline house before I sell it?

It depends on the work. Painting, tiling and replacing cabinets generally need no permit, but moving walls, doors or windows likely does, as does replacing a water heater. Email pcd@shorelinewa.gov with a description if you are unsure.

Am I responsible for unpermitted work a previous owner did?

Yes. Shoreline's permit guidance says the property owner is responsible for any work earlier owners did without permits. The city may require an investigation inspection permit before the building permit can be submitted, and permit fees may be doubled.

Can I remove a tree from my Shoreline lot before listing?

Only if the rules allow it. A tree that is an imminent hazard can be removed, and dead or dying trees outside critical areas have exemptions, but healthy trees may need a permit. Penalties for removing one without a permit can reach $15,000 or more.

Who supplies electricity and water in Shoreline?

Seattle City Light supplies electricity to all properties in the city. Water comes from Seattle Public Utilities or North City Water District depending on the address. Puget Sound Energy provides natural gas, and Recology handles garbage, recycling and compost.

How do I sell my house fast in Sammamish, WA?

The three usual routes in Sammamish are a standard listing, a sale by owner and a cash sale as-is. A cash sale is the one built for speed, because the buyer does not wait on a mortgage approval, but the price will reflect the condition of the house and the shortcut.

Sammamish is a high-value market. The Census Bureau's median value of owner-occupied housing for 2020 to 2024 is $1,407,300, and 82.6 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, so most sellers here own a single-family home on a plateau lot rather than a rental. The city's estimated population slipped 2.0 percent between the April 2020 base of 67,457 and 66,110 on July 1, 2025.

  • Hire an agent if the house shows well and you can handle a few weeks on the market.
  • Take a cash offer if you are relocating, settling an estate, or dealing with deferred maintenance.
  • Sell it yourself if you are comfortable preparing the disclosure form and the closing documents.

Whatever you choose, compare offers using the same four terms: price, closing date, closing cost split, and repair credits.

What kind of city is Sammamish?

Sammamish sits on a plateau east of Lake Sammamish about 20 miles east of Seattle, with the Snoqualmie Valley to the east. It covers 24.04 square miles, of which 3.61 are water, and neighbors Issaquah to the south, Redmond to the northwest and Bellevue across the lake. Beaver Lake and Pine Lake are the two largest lakes in the city, and Yellow Lake lies in the Klahanie area.

The plateau stayed mostly rural until suburban homes, shopping centers and schools arrived in the 1970s and 1980s. A 1991 vote to join Issaquah and a 1992 incorporation vote both failed. After frustration with county development rules, voters approved incorporation in 1998 and the city was officially incorporated on August 31, 1999. Sammamish annexed Klahanie on January 1, 2016.

The city approved plans for a denser Town Center in 2008. The first residential buildings were completed over the following decade, and construction on 38 townhomes in a later phase began in 2024, with more townhomes and 600 apartments planned. Sammamish does not have its own post office, the closest being in Redmond. Eastside Fire and Rescue provides fire service, and the city contracts with the King County Sheriff's Office for police.

Which schools and roads do Sammamish buyers ask about?

School district boundaries split the city along Southeast 8th Street. Everything north of it is in the Lake Washington School District, with Eastlake and Tesla STEM high schools and Inglewood and Renaissance middle schools. Everything south is in the Issaquah School District, with Issaquah and Skyline high schools and Beaver Lake, Pacific Cascade and Pine Lake middle schools. A small eastern area belongs to the Snoqualmie Valley School District. Say which district applies when you list the house, since buyers filter by it.

Major roads are East Lake Sammamish Parkway along the lakeshore, 228th Avenue through the business district and Issaquah-Pine Lake Road. State Route 202 leads to Redmond and Interstate 90 runs through Issaquah to the south. King County Metro runs a route linking Sammamish to Redmond, Issaquah and Mercer Island station, and the South Sammamish Park and Ride has 265 stalls. The 11-mile East Lake Sammamish Trail was completed in 2023.

The Census reports a mean travel time to work of 29.3 minutes, so commute questions are common. A buyer who works in Redmond will weigh the drive on SR 202, while one headed to Seattle will think about I-90 and the light rail connection at Mercer Island.

What do the Census numbers say about Sammamish households?

With 90.6 percent of residents in the same home a year earlier, turnover is low, and the buyers who do come are mostly families looking for space and schools. With 28.6 percent of residents under 18, bedroom count, yard size and the school district carry weight in pricing.

How does Sammamish weather and zoning affect a sale?

Winters are cool and wet, with the wettest months being November, December and January, and summers are warm and dry. Snowfall is rare. Recorded extremes run from minus 8 degrees Fahrenheit in February 1950 to 113 degrees in June 2021. Roof, gutters, drainage and crawl spaces get the most attention from inspectors, and the state disclosure form asks about roof leaks in the past five years, standing water and drainage problems.

Zoning details can add value. The city's R-4 zone allows up to 4 dwelling units per acre, a maximum floor area ratio of 50 percent for single-family homes and 40 percent hardscape coverage. A detached accessory dwelling unit in R-4 needs setbacks of 15 feet in front and 5 feet on the sides and rear, with a 24-foot height limit.

Accessory dwelling units are broadly allowed. Sammamish permits up to two on a lot with a detached single-family home, whether attached, detached or converted from an existing structure. A detached unit is capped at 1,000 square feet, and an attached unit can be up to 50 percent of the house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is larger. No extra parking is required when the property already has four or more spaces. If you are selling a lot with potential, mention these rules, and tell buyers to confirm current standards with the city.

What are the closing costs, taxes and disclosures in a Sammamish sale?

The state real estate excise tax is paid by the seller in most sales, due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the first $551,000 is taxed at 1.1 percent and the next slice up to $1,551,000 at 1.28 percent. At the Census median value of $1,407,300, that works out to $6,061 on the first bracket and $10,960.64 on the remaining $856,300, a state total of $17,021.64 before the local rate. This is an illustration of the arithmetic, not a quote. Ask your escrow officer or King County for the local rate and for the brackets that apply if you close before January 1.

Property tax bills follow the parcel. Under RCW 84.56.020, tax statements go out by March 15 when the county meets its deadlines, and each statement must describe the senior exemption and deferral programs. Half is due April 30 and half October 31 for bills of $50 or more. Treasurers may offer payment agreements for current or delinquent taxes, so ask King County Treasury about your balance before closing.

For the buyer's side of the file, give the disclosure statement within five business days of contract acceptance. It includes a notice that restrictive covenants based on race or other protected classes are void and unenforceable under RCW 49.60.224, and asks about homeowners' association dues, special assessments, shared common areas and recorded covenants. If your home is in an HOA, get the documents ready early.

A short checklist before you sign a contract:

  • The deed and loan payoff statement.
  • HOA bylaws, dues and any pending special assessments.
  • Permit and final inspection records for additions or any accessory unit.
  • The most recent King County property tax statement.

A cash sale can close as soon as title work is finished, and many sellers choose the date. A listing normally takes longer because of showings, inspections and buyer financing. Get the closing date in writing from any buyer.

Can I sell my Sammamish house as-is?

Yes. You can sell without making repairs, but you still need to complete the state disclosure form unless the buyer waives it or an exemption applies. A buyer who purchases as-is will account for the condition in the price.

Does the school district matter when I sell in Sammamish?

It matters to buyers. Addresses north of Southeast 8th Street are in the Lake Washington School District and those south are in the Issaquah School District, with a small eastern area in the Snoqualmie Valley district. Confirm the district for your address.

Can a buyer add an accessory dwelling unit to a Sammamish lot?

Often yes. The city allows up to two ADUs on a lot with a detached single-family home, with a 1,000 square foot maximum for a detached unit. Setbacks and height limits depend on the zone, so a buyer should confirm the standards with the city.

When are property taxes due on a Sammamish home?

Half is due April 30 and the remainder October 31, as RCW 84.56.020 provides for bills of $50 or more. King County Treasury collects the tax, and the closing agent usually prorates it between buyer and seller.

Can I sell my house fast in Richland, WA?

Yes. Richland sellers usually choose between a traditional listing, a sale without an agent, and a cash sale to a buyer who purchases as-is. The cash route is typically the quickest because no lender has to approve the buyer, though title work and your own paperwork still set the closing date.

Richland is in Benton County, in the Tri-Cities of southeastern Washington. Its numbers differ a lot from the Seattle area: the Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied home value of $436,700 for 2020 to 2024, and 64.4 percent of housing units are owner-occupied. The population has been growing, from 60,580 in the April 2020 estimates base to 65,258 on July 1, 2025, an increase of 7.7 percent.

  • A listing makes sense when the house is ready to show and you can wait for a buyer's loan.
  • A cash sale fits an inherited house, a rental with tenants, a house needing repairs, or a tight move date.
  • A sale by owner works if you can handle the contract, the seller disclosure form and the county excise tax affidavit.

Ask for each offer in writing, including the price, the closing date and who pays closing costs, so you can compare them fairly.

What is the history behind Richland's housing?

Much of Richland's older housing traces to World War II. The townsite was established in 1905 and named for Nelson Rich, and the city incorporated on April 28, 1910, as a small farm town. In 1943 the U.S. Army bought land along the Columbia River for the Manhattan Project, and on March 6, 1943 residents of Richland, White Bluffs and Hanford were evicted under a federal court order. The population rose from about 300 to 25,000 by the end of the war.

The Army planned the city, with Spokane architect Gustav Albin Pehrson overseeing the design. Prefabricated duplexes and single-family homes were built in many floor plans identified by letter, which is why they are called alphabet houses. Streets such as George Washington Way, Stevens Drive, Goethals Drive and Thayer Drive carry the names of engineers. The government owned the homes until the 1950s: Richland became a chartered first-class city on December 10, 1958, and the last government-owned home was sold on May 16, 1960.

If your house is one of these older homes, buyers may ask about the roof, wiring, insulation and any additions. The Gold Coast Historic District in north Richland, made up of houses built during the Cold War expansion, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2005, so check the status of a property in that area before you plan changes.

How does the Richland economy and climate affect sellers?

Richland's employment base is built around the Hanford cleanup mission, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (in Richland since 1965), Kadlec Regional Medical Center, Washington State University Tri-Cities and food processing, including Lamb Weston. The area is also a center of Columbia Valley wine production. Stable institutional employers tend to keep demand for housing steady, though buyers shop on price, commute and the yard.

The climate is semi-arid. Richland receives about 7 inches of precipitation a year, summers are hot and winters are milder than elsewhere in Eastern Washington. The city reached 118 degrees Fahrenheit during the 2021 heat wave. Heat shows up in a home inspection: expect questions about the air conditioner's age, attic insulation, roof condition and irrigation systems. Lawns and landscaping in this shrub-steppe setting usually depend on irrigation water, which the next section covers.

Schools come up in most buyer conversations. The Richland School District serves Richland and West Richland with ten elementary schools, four middle schools and three high schools. For commuting, I-82 runs west of the city and I-182 links Richland with Kennewick and Pasco.

The commute of 20.4 minutes is shorter than in Renton or Sammamish, which is a selling point worth stating in your listing or when you talk to buyers.

How do Benton County property taxes work when I sell?

The Benton County Treasurer collects property tax for the county, cities, school districts and other taxing districts, and the bill follows the property. Taxes are due when the treasurer certifies them, normally mid to late January. The first half is late if unpaid after April 30, and the second half is late after October 31. When a due date lands on a weekend, it moves to the following Monday, and a payment is on time if postmarked by the due date.

For residential property with four or fewer units, RCW 84.56.020 sets interest at 9 percent a year on delinquent tax and bars additional penalties. Benton County will not foreclose until real property is a full three years delinquent. The Treasurer's FAQ also notes that the county sends statements only at the start of the year, based on ownership on December 1 of the prior year, and that the closing is where you decide how the tax is handled. Ask the title company to confirm the balance before you sign.

Some Richland parcels also carry irrigation assessments collected on the tax bill. Benton Irrigation District, Columbia Irrigation District and Kiona Irrigation District bill through the Treasurer, while Kennewick Irrigation District must be paid directly to the district. Check which one serves your address.

Owners aged 61 or older, or retired because of a disability, may qualify for a senior or disabled exemption, and deferral is also possible. Those programs run through the Benton County Assessor at (509) 735-2394. Valuation appeals go to the Benton County Board of Equalization.

What paperwork does a Richland closing require?

Every transfer of title in Benton County needs a Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit with the deed. The Treasurer will not accept the affidavit unless sections 1 through 7 are complete, and mobile homes need a separate affidavit. Forms are available online and at both Treasurer locations, 620 Market Street in Prosser and 7122 W Okanogan Place in Kennewick. The seller usually pays the tax, which is due on the date of sale, and the Department of Revenue treats the date the deed is notarized as that date.

For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state rate is 1.1 percent up to $551,000. At Richland's Census median value of $436,700, the state portion would be $4,803.70 before the local rate. This is only an illustration of the arithmetic. Ask your escrow officer or the Benton County Treasurer for the local rate and for the brackets that apply if you close before the new year.

Separately, the seller disclosure statement under RCW 64.06.020 is due within five business days after contract acceptance, and the buyer has three business days after delivery to rescind. The form includes sections on household water, irrigation water rights, sewer or on-site systems and wood-burning appliances, all of which come up in Richland's mix of city and rural-edge lots. Permit history matters too: the City of Richland issues building permits through its online permitting system, which went live on June 3, 2024, and its Building Division is at 625 Swift Boulevard.

  • Any irrigation district bill or water rights paperwork tied to the lot.

A cash sale can close as soon as title work is done, often on a date you set. A listing takes longer because of showings, inspections and the buyer's financing. Request the closing date in writing from any buyer.

The first half is due by April 30 and the second half by October 31. If the first half is late, interest starts running. A payment postmarked by the due date counts as on time. Interest on residential property with four or fewer units follows RCW 84.56.020.

Do I owe the real estate excise tax when I sell in Richland?

Usually yes. The seller normally pays, according to the Department of Revenue, and it is due on the date of sale to the county treasurer. A completed affidavit must accompany the deed in Benton County.

Can I sell a Richland house that needs repairs?

Yes. You can sell as-is, but answer the state disclosure form honestly about roof leaks, structural defects, water and sewer systems and permits. A buyer who purchases as-is will adjust the offer for the condition.

Where do I ask about a senior property tax exemption in Richland?

Ask the Benton County Assessor, who administers the senior and disabled exemptions and deferral programs. The Treasurer's office cannot change the amount due until the Assessor approves the application, so keep paying the bill by its due dates.

How do you sell a house fast in Lakewood, WA?

A Lakewood owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept an as-is cash offer, and the right choice depends on the house and on how it is being used. A vacant, well-kept house suits a listing. A house with tenants, deferred repairs or an estate attached tends to move faster in a direct sale.

Fewer than half of Lakewood homes are owner-occupied. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 47.5 percent for 2020 to 2024, the median gross rent at $1,525 and the median value of owner-occupied homes at $461,200. The city also has a registration and inspection program for rentals, covered below, which shapes how a rented house sells.

How did Lakewood become a city, and how is it laid out?

Lakewood was incorporated on February 28, 1996, the same day as Edgewood, after voters had turned down incorporation in 1971, 1990 and 1994. It became the second largest city in Pierce County at once. The city has 17.06 square miles of land and several lakes.

  • American Lake: the largest, at 1,091 acres and an average depth of 53 feet.
  • Lake Steilacoom, Gravelly Lake, Lake Louise and Waughop Lake: the other named lakes, with Waughop Lake inside Fort Steilacoom Park.
  • Chambers Creek: the largest creek, flowing from Lake Steilacoom toward Chambers Bay.

State Route 512 ends at its western terminus where it meets Interstate 5 in Lakewood. Pierce Transit is headquartered in the city, and the Lakewood Sounder station, which opened in 2012 as the southern end of the S Line, runs commuter trains north through Tacoma to Seattle. Census data put the mean commute at 29.3 minutes.

What drives Lakewood's economy and local services?

Joint Base Lewis-McChord, a military installation with about 55,000 employees, sits beside the city, and the local economy is closely tied to it. Lakewood had 30,662 full-time jobs in 2023, with more than 9,000 of them in health care. St. Clare Hospital was the largest employer at 598 employees, and the city recorded $1.65 billion in taxable retail sales in 2022. The Census Bureau counts 6,594 veterans among residents.

Public services are split among several providers, which matters when you fill in disclosure forms or hand over utility accounts:

  • The Clover Park School District runs the public schools for most of the city, and parts of Lakewood sit in the Steilacoom Historical and Tacoma districts.
  • Electricity comes from Lakeview Light and Power on the east side, Tacoma Power on the north side and Puget Sound Energy on the west side, which is also the only natural gas provider.
  • The Lakewood Water District supplies tap water to 17,680 connections.
  • Pierce County Public Works and Utilities maintains sanitary sewer, and the city manages stormwater.
  • The Lakewood Police Department began independent operations on November 1, 2004, and West Pierce Fire and Rescue covers the city.

Which Lakewood landmarks and campuses do buyers recognize?

Fort Steilacoom Park holds Waughop Lake, and Western State Hospital, a 745-bed state psychiatric hospital, stands on the site of the old Fort Steilacoom. Lakewold Gardens, Thornewood, the Lakewood Playhouse (founded 1938) and the Lakewood Towne Center round out the local landmarks. Pierce College Fort Steilacoom and Clover Park Technical College are the two campuses in the city.

Health care includes St. Clare Hospital, which began as Lakewood General Hospital in 1961, and the VA American Lake Medical Center, which opened in 1924 as a veterans hospital. The Pierce County Library System has served Lakewood since the area was annexed in 1996, and its interim library location opened in September 2024.

How does Lakewood's Rental Housing Safety Program affect a sale?

The city's Rental Housing Safety Program requires owners of rental property to register every year, and registered properties are inspected once every five years. An initial inspection may be done by a city inspector or by a qualified private inspector, and every re-inspection is done by the city. Inspectors look at structural integrity, weather exposure, plumbing and sanitation, heat and water, ventilation, electrical wiring, exits, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.

An owner who fails to register can face penalties under the city's fee schedule and the Lakewood Municipal Code, and a rental business license can be revoked. A buyer of a rented house will ask for registration and inspection records, so gather them before you list. Exemptions under LMC 5.60.025 include:

  • Units occupied by the owner, or by the owner's parent or child.
  • Mobile and manufactured homes, shelters and transitional housing.
  • Condominiums and townhouses in multi-unit structures under multiple ownership, unless one owner holds them.
  • Units built in the past 10 years with a certificate of occupancy and no code violations.

Renting rooms in a home you live in does not require registration, but moving out and renting the whole house does. Contact the program at 253-512-2261 or rentals@cityoflakewood.us.

What are Lakewood's short-term rental rules?

Short-term rentals of under 30 days are allowed in most zones. The city excludes Commercial 1 to 3, the Industrial Business Park, Industrial 1 and 2, Public and Semi-Public Institutional and Open Space Recreation 1 and 2. A short-term rental must register with the Rental Housing Safety Program, hold a business license, renew annually and be inspected every five years, with a free first inspection. The city handles the permit as a Type II administrative decision. Check your zoning before you promise a buyer short-term rental income.

When are Pierce County property taxes due for a Lakewood house?

Tax statements go out in February. If the amount is more than $50 it may be paid in two installments, April 30 and October 31, and an amount of $50 or less is due in full on April 30. Pierce County says that if a payment envelope is postmarked before the statutory deadline, interest and penalty are waived. October 31, 2026 fell on a Saturday, and the second-half deadline has now passed.

Pay online or at the Assessor-Treasurer's Office, 2401 S. 35th St., Room 142, Tacoma, which also has a drop box. Foreclosure avoidance payments go by cashier's check to that office. For status, call the Assessor-Treasurer hotline at (253) 798-6111. Mortgage companies follow the same payment rules as the owner.

What does a Lakewood seller owe and disclose at closing?

The seller normally pays the state real estate excise tax, which the Department of Revenue says is due on the sale date, and a city local tax is added. The graduated state rate starts at 1.1 percent on the first slice of the price under RCW 82.45.060, and the thresholds change January 1, 2027. On a sale at the $461,200 median value, the first-slice rate would give about $5,073 in state tax before the local portion.

The disclosure form under RCW 64.06.020 asks about the sewer connection, roof leaks and environmental items. The buyer has three business days after delivery to rescind unless the contract provides otherwise.

Registration is required each year while the house is rented, unless an exemption applies. A buyer will want the certificate and inspection history, so register and inspect first if you have not.

Yes. A buyer who keeps the tenant will look at the city's rental registration and inspection records. Ask a Washington attorney how your lease and notice requirements apply.

The seller usually pays, according to the Department of Revenue, and the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. If it goes unpaid, interest accrues from the sale date.

How is Lacey laid out, and why does it matter to a seller?

Lacey lies between Olympia on the west and the Nisqually River delta on the east. Its northern edge reaches the Nisqually Reach of Puget Sound beside Tolmie State Park, and the BNSF Seattle Subdivision forms much of the southern boundary. The city covers 17.2 square miles of land.

Interstate 5 runs west to east through the middle of the city, so location relative to the freeway affects commute and noise. A few road and transit facts a buyer will weigh:

  • Intercity Transit runs the county bus system, and Lacey is the eastern end of its bus rapid transit route, The One.
  • Centennial Station, the only Amtrak stop in Thurston County, sits near Lacey's southern edge and sees Cascades and Coast Starlight trains.
  • The city maintained 178.6 miles of streets as of 2021.

The mean commute for Lacey workers is 25.4 minutes, according to the Census Bureau.

What shaped Lacey's history and economy?

Settlers Isaac and Catherine Wood claimed land in 1853 and the place was first called Woodland. When the community applied for a post office in 1891 the name was taken, and Lacey was chosen. Voters rejected incorporation in 1964 and approved it in 1966, and the city was officially incorporated on December 5, 1966.

The South Sound Center opened in 1966 and remains the largest retail area. Lacey designated 500 acres in Hawks Prairie for industrial use in the 1990s, and the area filled with warehouses and distribution centers, including a Target facility of about 1.7 million square feet that opened in 2003. The Nisqually Tribe announced plans in 2023 for the Quiemuth Resort casino and 350-room hotel next to Lacey Gateway.

The whole city is inside North Thurston Public Schools, with North Thurston, River Ridge and Timberline high schools and Chinook, Komachin, Nisqually and Salish middle schools. Saint Martin's University, founded in 1895, is in Lacey, and South Puget Sound Community College has a branch campus here. Providence St. Peter Hospital, the county's largest at 372 beds, sits just northwest of the city.

When are Thurston County property taxes due, and what if they are late?

The Thurston County Treasurer explains what happens when a payment is missed:

  • If the first half is not paid by April 30, the whole year's tax is treated as late and interest runs on the full amount.
  • A 3 percent penalty may be added on June 1 and another 8 percent on December 1.
  • The county does not grant extensions for hardship, and a late payment must include the added charges or it is returned.
  • Real property is not sold for unpaid tax until the taxes are three full years delinquent, and a payment plan is available for delinquent prior-year taxes.

Pay at the Treasurer's office, 3000 Pacific Ave SE, Suite 130, Olympia, or call 360-786-5550. If your lender pays your taxes, the county sends a postcard each February, but the owner remains legally responsible. Clear any unpaid balance before you list, since a title company will find it.

The state rate is graduated, and a city local rate is added; RCW 82.46.010 authorizes city excise taxes within a statutory cap. After delivery the buyer has three business days to rescind unless the contract says otherwise in writing. Lacey sellers with a house served by a septic system should answer the on-site sewage questions carefully, since they cover tanks, drainfields and whether fixtures connect to the system.

A Lacey business license is required to operate a business in the city, and it is applied for through the state Department of Revenue by adding a City of Lacey endorsement to a state registration. The city also requires annual registration of any complex with five or more rental dwelling units. The city describes that program for complexes of that size, so ask the city whether anything else applies to a single rented house.

Work that changes how a building is used needs a city permit under the construction permit rules, and applications go through the city's online portal. What should a seller know about Olympia, Washington?

Olympia is the capital of Washington and the county seat of Thurston County. It sits at the southern end of Puget Sound on Budd Inlet, about 47 miles southwest of Seattle, and shares borders with Lacey and Tumwater. The Census Bureau estimates 56,724 residents as of July 1, 2025, which is 2.4% above the April 2020 estimates base.

Much of downtown sits on reclaimed land, and the Deschutes River was dammed in 1951 to form Capitol Lake. The state approved removing that dam in late 2022. A house near the water or on fill can draw questions about soil and drainage, so gather any past inspection reports before you list.

Olympia has a council-manager government and its own permit center at City Hall, 601 4th Avenue E. Most sellers deal with the city only if they have open permits, a rental, or a lot that could take more housing. The sections below cover those points, then the state and county steps every Olympia sale goes through.

How does Olympia's weather affect a house for sale?

Olympia is wet, cloudy and mild. It averages about 50 inches of precipitation a year with roughly 75% cloud cover, and November through January are the rainiest months. City streets, creeks and rivers can flood between November and February.

Summer heat is rarer but real: the record high is 110 degrees, set on June 28, 2021, and an average of 6.3 days a year reach 90 degrees. Snow averages around 10.8 inches a season, though it has ranged from a trace to 81.5 inches in 1968 to 1969.

Buyers walking an Olympia house tend to look at the same few things:

  • Roof, gutters and downspouts, since the wet season runs for months.
  • Crawlspace and basement moisture, especially in older homes near the inlet or on fill.
  • Moss, rot and drainage around the foundation.
  • Cooling or ventilation, now that summers can reach the 90s and beyond.

Fixing or documenting these items before a showing shortens the inspection phase. A buyer taking the house as-is still reads the seller disclosure, so answer those questions accurately.

Which Olympia city rules matter when you sell?

Olympia allows up to two accessory dwelling units on almost all lots. Each can be up to 1,000 square feet and 24 feet tall, attached or detached. The city also allows middle housing in every residential zone: up to four units on a lot when zoning standards are met, and up to six within a half mile of frequent transit routes or when at least two units stay affordable for 50 years.

That flexibility can raise what a lot is worth to a builder or investor, so mention it if your lot is large. The city also offers six pre-approved ADU plans on its middle housing page.

Rental owners have a few extra steps. The state Department of Revenue's Olympia endorsement page says the city may require rental registration and, for short-term vacation rentals, an additional permit, both filed through the city's online permit portal. A general city business license costs $30 when reported gross income is above $4,000.

  • Permit Center: City Hall, second floor, 601 4th Avenue E, phone 360.753.8314.
  • Counter hours: Monday to Thursday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Fridays.
  • Inspections and permit status are handled through the city's online permit portal.

If an old project never got a final inspection, call the Permit Center before you list and ask what the permit record shows.

How much real estate excise tax does an Olympia seller pay?

The seller owes Washington's real estate excise tax, plus any local portion set for the city. RCW 82.45.080 makes the tax the seller's obligation. The state portion is graduated: 1.1% on the part of the price up to $525,000, 1.28% on the part from $525,000 to $1,525,000, 2.75% up to $3,025,000, and 3% above that.

The Department of Revenue lists new thresholds for sales beginning January 1, 2027: $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. At the Census median of $486,200, the state portion would be 1.1%, or about $5,348, before the local rate. Ask the Thurston County Treasurer for the local rate that applies to your address.

The tax is due on the date of sale, which the Department of Revenue defines as the date the deed is notarized, whether or not the deed is recorded that day. If the tax is not paid within one month of the sale date, interest applies. The affidavit, deed and payment go to the county treasurer where the property sits. More detail is on the Department of Revenue REET page.

How do Thurston County property taxes work at closing?

Thurston County bills property tax in two halves. The first half is due April 30 and the balance is due October 31, and a due date that lands on a weekend moves to the following Monday. In 2026 the second-half date fell on a Saturday, so it moved to Monday, November 2, which has now passed.

Taxes follow the property, not the owner, and the county does not send new statements when a house changes hands. The Treasurer's FAQ says it is your responsibility to decide how taxes are handled in your closing and to know whether the property still has taxes due for the year. Ask your closing agent to prorate the current year and to pay any unpaid half from sale proceeds.

Sellers who are 61 or older, or retired from a disability, may have a tax reduction or a deferral. Those programs run through the Thurston County Assessor, at 360-867-2200 per the Treasurer's FAQ. A deferral is repaid from the estate, so confirm the payoff with the county before closing.

  • Treasurer's office: 3000 Pacific Avenue SE, Suite 130, Olympia, phone 360-786-5550.
  • Special charges such as stormwater can appear on the same bill and are liens too.
  • Real property is not sold for unpaid tax until three full years of delinquency.

What does an Olympia seller have to hand the buyer?

For a sale of improved residential property, the seller must deliver a completed disclosure statement, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt. RCW 64.06.020 sets the form and says delivery must happen within five business days of a mutual acceptance unless the parties agree otherwise.

The buyer then has three business days after delivery to rescind. If you do not provide the statement, the buyer may instead waive the right to rescind before or after the contract. Complete every line, write NA where a question does not apply, and explain any yes answer on an attached sheet.

Disclosure covers what you actually know. Past roof leaks, drainage problems and permit history in an older Olympia house all belong on the form if you know of them.

What are the ways to sell a house in Olympia?

Most Olympia owners choose among three routes, and the same deed, excise tax and tax proration steps apply to each.

  • List with a real estate agent and accept the time showings, repairs and buyer financing take.
  • Sell on your own, which means handling the disclosure form, the contract and the closing paperwork yourself.
  • Take an as-is offer from a cash buyer, which can cut repairs and financing delays, though the price usually sits below a fully prepared listing.

Compare written offers, ask what each buyer expects you to pay at closing, and keep the deed and affidavit timing in mind so the sale date and tax payment line up.

More questions about Olympia, WA

How much is the excise tax when I sell a house in Olympia?

It depends on the price and the local rate. The state portion is 1.1% on the first $525,000 of the sale, 1.28% on the next slice up to $1,525,000, and higher above that, with new thresholds starting January 1, 2027. The Thurston County Treasurer can tell you the local rate for your address.

When are Thurston County property taxes due?

The first half is due April 30 and the second half is due October 31, with weekend dates moving to the next Monday. The 2026 second-half deadline was Monday, November 2, so it has passed. The next first-half deadline is April 30, 2027.

Can I build an extra unit on my Olympia lot before selling?

Often yes. Olympia allows up to two ADUs on almost all lots, each up to 1,000 square feet and 24 feet tall, and middle housing of up to four units in residential zones when standards are met. Call the Permit Center at 360.753.8314 to check your lot before you start.

Who pays the real estate excise tax in Washington, buyer or seller?

The seller. RCW 82.45.080 makes it the seller's obligation, though the buyer can become responsible if the seller does not pay, and unpaid tax can become a lien on the property.

Where do I file the excise tax affidavit for an Olympia house?

With the Thurston County Treasurer, together with the deed and payment, because the tax is paid to the treasurer of the county where the property sits. Your closing or escrow officer normally handles this at signing.

The first homestead claims came in 1870, and David Bothell and his family platted the town in 1888. Bothell incorporated in 1909, lived on logging and farming at first, and became a bedroom community for Seattle commuters in the mid-20th century. Interstate 405 now links it to the rest of the Eastside, and downtown has been redeveloped since the 2010s with denser housing.

Many north-south streets change numbers when they cross it. The city annexed Canyon Park in 1992, and that move carried the limits into Snohomish County.

Look at the property tax statement to see which county bills the house. What drives buyer demand in Bothell?

Jobs drive it. Since the 1980s the Canyon Park and North Creek business districts have turned Bothell into a regional employment center, and the city has the second-largest biotechnology hub in Washington, with 61 companies and about 4,000 employees. Pfizer's Seagen, AGC Biologics and Fujifilm Sonosite are among the names there. The University of Washington Bothell and Cascadia College share a campus east of downtown, with about 6,000 students at the university as of 2019.

A 2022 city study found that among Bothell residents who work elsewhere, 29 percent go to Seattle, 14 percent to Bellevue, 12 percent to Redmond and 8 percent to Kirkland, and that 26 percent of residents work from home. Highway access matters to those buyers: Interstate 405 meets State Route 522 here, and State Routes 524 and 527 serve the north. Community Transit routes from the Canyon Park hub, including the Swift Green Line, connect Bothell to Lynnwood, Mill Creek and Everett.

Which Bothell neighborhoods and schools should a listing mention?

Bothell's comprehensive plan sorts the city into planning subareas, and about 41 percent of its land is zoned for single-family homes.

  • Downtown Bothell lies north of the Sammamish River between Westhill and Interstate 405.
  • Canyon Park and North Creek are commercial and industrial districts with office parks and warehouses.
  • Maywood and Beckstrom Hill sit north of downtown, east of the Bothell-Everett Highway.
  • Waynita, Simonds and Norway Hill cover the neighborhoods south of the river and west of the freeway.
  • Brickyard Road and Queensgate occupy the southeast corner.

The Northshore School District serves Bothell and runs 35 schools, 12 of them inside the city. Bothell High School occupies a West Hill campus completed in 1953 and renovated in 2008, and Inglemoor and North Creek high schools also draw Bothell students. The city's hills include slopes south of the Sammamish River that are prone to landslides, and wetlands and creeks run through town, so ask the city whether a lot touches a critical area.

What permits and city rules matter if you sell a Bothell house?

The Permit Center takes permit and land use applications online only, through MyBuildingPermit.com, and answers questions at 425-806-6400 or permits@bothellwa.gov. New zoning rules took effect on January 1, 2025 under BMC 12.14, and the city's CobMap tool shows a parcel's zoning and environmental layers. A buyer planning to add a unit or split a lot should check that map first.

  • Cutting a tree generally needs no permit on an existing lot under 20,000 square feet when there are no wetlands, streams, steep slopes over 40 percent or shoreline designation.
  • Construction noise is limited to 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturdays.
  • If your home's final inspection was more than 90 days ago, the city may not have the plans on file.

Ask the Permit Center whether the house has any open permits, and whether a rental or accessory unit is allowed on the lot, before you sign a contract.

What does a Bothell seller owe at closing?

The seller owes real estate excise tax. RCW 82.45.060 sets four state bands that run from 1.1 percent at the bottom to 3 percent at the top, and the current break points are $525,000, $1,525,000 and $3,025,000. At the Census median value of $925,100, the state portion is $10,896: $5,775 on the first $525,000 plus 1.28 percent of the remaining $400,100. The local portion is added on top, and RCW 82.46.010 lets cities and counties impose local layers of up to 0.25 percent and an additional layer of up to 0.5 percent.

RCW 82.45.080 makes the tax the seller's obligation. Payment is due at the time of sale, and RCW 82.45.100 adds interest after one month plus penalties that climb to 20 percent at three months. The buyer becomes personally liable for unpaid tax if the deed is not recorded, and the county wants the tax paid before recording. Ask the closing agent for the exact total for your parcel.

When are property taxes due on a Bothell house?

Washington law makes first-half taxes due April 30 and second-half taxes due October 31. Snohomish County mails statements in mid-February and warns that mail processing can run until May 15 or November 15 during heavy volume. It also offers an interest and penalty waiver after the death of a taxpayer and tax reductions for seniors and disabled owners, which the Assessor's Office at 425-388-3540 can explain. For a King County parcel, call the county's Treasury Operations to confirm the amount before you sell.

Residential property with four or fewer units carries nine percent annual interest on late tax under RCW 84.56.020. Check that no balance is delinquent before you list.

What are your options for selling a Bothell house quickly?

With a median value above $900,000, carrying costs add up while a house sits, so compare the routes before you choose.

  • List with an agent and prepare the house for showings.
  • Sell without an agent and manage the disclosure and the paperwork yourself.
  • Request a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house as-is, which fits an inherited property, a house with deferred repairs or a move with a firm deadline.

Do I need a permit to cut a tree before I sell my Bothell house?

Usually not on a lot under 20,000 square feet with no wetlands, streams, steep slopes over 40 percent or shoreline designation. Contact a city planner at planning@bothellwa.gov if you are unsure.

Who supplies electricity and water to Bothell homes?

It depends on the side of the county line and the neighborhood. Puget Sound Energy or the Snohomish County PUD supplies power, and one of four water districts supplies water, so confirm both before you schedule final readings.

Gottlieb Burian settled beside what is now Lake Burien in 1884, and the area grew from a trail-served community into a suburb. A 2010 annexation of the southern part of North Highline, with 14,292 residents, lifted the population past 52,000 and made Burien the 25th largest city in the state. Burien borders Seattle and the unincorporated communities of White Center and Boulevard Park on the north, Tukwila and SeaTac on the east, and Normandy Park on the south. Where a house sits within that frame affects how buyers describe it.

  • Olde Burien surrounds Southwest 152nd Street on the west side of Ambaum Boulevard, and Town Square, completed in 2017, holds shops, condominiums, apartments, a senior living center, a King County library branch and City Hall.
  • Ambaum Boulevard follows the old Lake Burien Railway route, which opened in 1915 and carried a small passenger train to Seattle.

The Highline School District serves Burien, with Highline High School, Big Picture, CHOICE Academy and the Puget Sound Skills Center. Confirm the school assignment for the address before you quote it in a listing.

How do roads and transit help sell a Burien house?

Burien sits at the junction of State Routes 509 and 518, immediately northwest of the airport, and Ambaum Boulevard and Des Moines Memorial Drive carry traffic to the north. King County Metro and Sound Transit run buses from the Burien Transit Center, which opened in June 2009, to Seattle, Bellevue, the airport, West Seattle, Kent, Auburn, Renton, Des Moines and Tukwila. The Census Bureau puts the mean commute at 26.7 minutes. Buyers who work near the airport or downtown Seattle will weigh that against the price, so lead with the transit and freeway access when you describe the house.

Which Burien rental rules apply when you sell a house with tenants?

Burien's rental rules affect a seller whose house has a renter in it. The city requires an annual rental housing business license, handled by the state Business Licensing Service, but single-family residences, condos, townhomes, manufactured homes and accessory dwelling units are exempt. For other rentals, the 2026 fee per complex is $323.80 for 1 to 10 units, $809.50 for 11 to 50 units and $971.41 for 51 or more.

  • Under the Rental Housing Policy in BMC 5.63, a landlord needs one of a list of just causes to evict, and wanting to sell the unit counts only after the tenant gets at least 90 days' written notice.
  • A landlord cannot evict from a unit that lacks a required license, or whose required inspection was not finished by the deadline.
  • The inspection program, in place since 2021, requires at least 20 percent of covered units to be inspected every three years.
  • Owners of buildings with five or more units that rent at affordable levels must give the city 60 calendar days' written notice before listing the building for sale.

State law also limits rent increases (RCW 59.18.700 and 59.18.720). The city's rental housing program answers questions at (206) 241-4647.

Washington also requires a seller of improved residential property to deliver a completed disclosure statement within five business days after the contract is mutually accepted, unless the buyer waived it or the transfer is exempt. The buyer then has three business days to rescind (RCW 64.06.020). The form covers title, water, structural items, systems and fixtures and environmental questions, so gather permits and repair records before you start.

When are property taxes due on a Burien house?

State law sets the dates. First-half taxes are due on or before April 30 and second-half taxes on or before October 31, under RCW 84.56.020. Residential property with four or fewer units picks up nine percent annual interest when it is delinquent, and the statute allows no penalties on that class of property. Ask King County Treasury Operations for the current amount and any balance due before you list. Each tax statement must also describe the senior and disabled exemption (RCW 84.36.379 through 84.36.389) and the deferral program in chapter 84.38 RCW.

What are your options for selling a Burien house quickly?

A seller with a tight timeline, a tenant in place or a house that needs work usually compares three routes.

No. Burien exempts single-family residences, condominiums, townhomes, manufactured homes and accessory dwelling units from the annual rental housing business license. Other eviction and notice rules in BMC 5.63 can still apply.

Can I end a tenancy in Burien because I am selling the house?

Yes, but only with at least 90 days' written notice, because selling the unit is one of the just causes in BMC 5.63.070. Without a valid cause, the city rules do not allow the eviction.

The state portion is about $7,232, which is 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 plus 1.28 percent on the remaining $113,800. The local portion is added on top.

A completed seller disclosure statement, delivered within five business days after both sides accept the contract, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt. The buyer then has three business days to rescind.

April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. Delinquent residential tax with four or fewer units carries nine percent annual interest.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, Bremerton city.

How do the shipyard, ferries and bridges shape buyer demand in Bremerton?

Commute routes decide which Bremerton blocks sell fastest. The Port Washington Narrows cuts the city in two, and two bridges join the halves: the Warren Avenue Bridge on State Route 303, opened in 1958, and the Manette Bridge, rebuilt in 2011. State Route 3 runs as a freeway through the west side and a tunnel carries ferry traffic from the terminal to State Route 304.

Washington State Ferries takes about an hour from Bremerton to Seattle, and in 2024 that route carried 990,435 passengers. Kitsap Transit's passenger-only fast ferry covers the crossing in 28 minutes. Buyers who work at the shipyard or across the water may ask how far a house sits from the terminal or the gates.

  • Downtown and the waterfront have new apartments, restored older buildings and the Admiral Theatre.
  • Manette sits on its own peninsula, was annexed in 1918 and reaches downtown over the Manette Bridge.
  • Charleston grew as a sailors' town, joined the city in 1927 and centers on Callow Avenue.
  • Union Hill is mostly residential and lies between downtown and Charleston.
  • Evergreen has water views and a park with a beach and boat ramp.
  • Haddon surrounds Bremerton High School and the Olympic College campus.

Three school districts reach into the city: Bremerton, Central Kitsap and South Kitsap. Confirm the district for your address before you put it in a listing.

How does Bremerton weather affect an older house?

Bremerton has warm, dry summers and wet, mild winters. Rainfall averages 56.93 inches a year, while snow averages about 3 inches. The wettest year on record, 1999, brought 75.81 inches. With that much water, roofs, gutters, siding, crawl spaces and drainage deserve attention before a showing or an inspection. The city sits in USDA climate zone 8.

What does the Bremerton landlord license mean for a seller?

Anyone who rents or leases real property inside Bremerton limits needs a City of Bremerton Landlord Business License under BMC 3.48.025. It is a city license, separate from any Washington state business license, and it costs $75 a year. Licenses run January 1 through December 31 and renewals are due by January 31.

  • Renting rooms inside your own home counts as rental activity.
  • A relative living in the house counts as a rental even without rent, unless the owner also lives there more than half the year.
  • Landlords join the Landlord Notification Program (BMC 5.06) by giving the Police Department a list of rentals and a contact method.
  • Landlords certify that units meet RCW 59.18.060, and the city does not run physical inspections.
  • Stays under 30 days, such as vacation rentals, fall under state business licensing instead.

The city warns that an unlicensed property may limit the owner's ability to pursue an eviction. If you inherited a Bremerton rental, bring the license in line before you list it, and call the Tax and License Division at 360-473-5311 with questions.

What does a Bremerton seller owe at closing?

The seller pays real estate excise tax, and the Kitsap County Treasurer collects it. Kitsap lists the local portion at 0.50 percent, and the state portion is graduated. On a sale at the Census median value of $439,400, the state portion is 1.1 percent of the full price, or $4,833.40, because the price sits under the $525,000 first band. The local 0.50 percent adds $2,197, for about $7,030 in total, plus a $5 state technology fee. Ask the treasurer to confirm the total for your parcel.

  • The tax is due within 30 days of the date on the conveying document and must be paid before the deed can be recorded.
  • The Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit must be signed by seller and buyer, or by an agent for each.
  • The treasurer takes cash or check payable to the Kitsap County Treasurer, and cards carry fees.
  • Late payment adds interest and penalties under RCW 82.45.100, which reach 20 percent of the tax after three months.

For sales starting January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue moves the state break points to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000.

How does Kitsap County bill property tax to Bremerton owners?

Kitsap County bills in two halves. The first is due April 30 and the balance October 31, payments count if postmarked by those dates, and a bill of $50 or less is due in full in April. For residential property with four or fewer units, delinquent tax carries interest of 0.75 percent a month, which matches the nine percent a year in RCW 84.56.020. There is no general good cause waiver. Failing to receive a statement does not erase interest.

Escrow deserves a look. Kitsap warns that tax money collected at a refinance is sometimes not forwarded to the treasurer until April or October, so confirm the account shows as paid before you list. The Assessor's Office, reachable at (360) 337-5777, handles the senior and disabled exemption and deferral, the limited-income deferral, the residential improvement exemption and the destroyed property exemption. State law also bars interest and penalties on the home of an active duty service member stationed outside the United States during a period of armed conflict.

What are your options for selling a Bremerton house quickly?

Orders to a new duty station, an inherited rental or a house that needs work all push owners toward a faster sale. The routes are familiar.

  • List with an agent and time showings around the weekend crowds that fill downtown for events such as the Armed Forces Day parade in May and the Blackberry Festival over Labor Day.
  • Sell the house yourself, handling the disclosure statement and the excise tax affidavit on your own.
  • Request a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is, which can avoid repairs and open houses.

Whichever route you choose, hand the buyer the seller disclosure statement within five business days after the contract is signed unless it is waived or exempt, since RCW 64.06.020 gives the buyer three business days to rescind once it arrives.

More questions about Bremerton, WA

How much does a Bremerton seller pay in excise tax?

It depends on the price. The state portion starts at 1.1 percent on the first $525,000, and Kitsap County lists the local portion at 0.50 percent. At $439,400 that comes to about $7,030, plus a $5 state technology fee.

Does Bremerton require a license to rent out a house?

Yes. Anyone renting real property inside city limits needs a Bremerton Landlord Business License, which costs $75 a year and renews by January 31. The city does not inspect the unit and relies on the landlord's certification.

When are Kitsap County property taxes due?

April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. Payments must be postmarked by those dates, and a bill of $50 or less is due in full on April 30.

Can I sell a Bremerton house I inherited with tenants inside?

Yes, but confirm the Landlord Business License is current first, because an unlicensed property can limit the owner's eviction options. Review the lease and ask the Tax and License Division at 360-473-5311 about the license record.

How can I confirm a house is inside Bremerton city limits?

Enter the address in the Kitsap County Parcel Search, the tool the city points owners to. City limits decide whether the landlord license and other city rules apply.

What should I know about selling a house in Edmonds, WA?

Edmonds is a Puget Sound waterfront city in southwest Snohomish County, about 15 miles north of Seattle, and the population is older than most Puget Sound suburbs. The Census Bureau estimates 42,748 residents as of July 1, 2025, close to the 42,853 counted in 2020, so the city has barely grown in five years.

That profile shapes who sells and why. Nearly a quarter of residents are 65 or older, 70.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied and 88.2 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Typical sale triggers are downsizing, an inherited house, a move closer to family and rental properties that owners want to exit. Each of those carries its own paperwork, which the sections below walk through. Edmonds also has about five miles of Puget Sound shoreline and a regional arts scene downtown, which keeps buyers interested in close-in homes.

What do Census numbers say about Edmonds homes?

How does Edmonds geography affect a house sale?

Edmonds is a set of hillside neighborhoods around a downtown valley, so location inside the city matters to buyers. It was platted in 1884 and incorporated on August 14, 1890, making it the oldest incorporated city in Snohomish County. Early work was in shingle mills and logging, and the hills around the downtown valley were built out as suburbs from the 1950s on and later annexed. The result is a city of distinct pockets:

  • Downtown and the Bowl: a valley with views of Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains, close to the beach, the fishing pier and the ferry dock.
  • Five Corners, Firdale, Perrinville, Seaview, Sherwood and Westgate: hillside neighborhoods, several with their own small commercial centers.
  • The State Route 99 corridor: the eastern commercial edge, home to the city's car dealerships.
  • Esperance: an unincorporated enclave in the southeast corner that has resisted annexation, so confirm whether an address is inside city limits.

Transportation is a selling point. The Washington State Ferries route runs to Kingston, the downtown station is served by Amtrak and Sounder, and Community Transit buses reach outlying areas. Only about 11.7 percent of residents work inside the city, and about 11 percent commute to Seattle, which is why buyers ask about transit and drive times first.

Do Edmonds landlords need a license, and what about backyard units?

Yes. The City of Edmonds requires a business license for any business operating in the city, including property owners, and it places home rentals in the General Business License category. The city page lists a $186.87 application fee and a $74.75 annual renewal. Applications run through the state Business Licensing Service on the Department of Revenue website, and the city follows up for a floor plan and supplemental questionnaire. Business Licensing can be reached at 425-775-2525.

A landlord selling a tenant-occupied house should confirm the license is current and tell the buyer what the lease says. For building questions, the Planning and Development Department is at 121 5th Ave N, phone 425-771-0220. The city runs a Pre-Approved DADU Plan Program for detached accessory dwelling units, though its page says no plans are in the catalog yet, so any existing backyard unit should come with permit records. The department's posted counter hours since September 2, 2025 are Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m., closed Wednesdays, with phone and digital help weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Confirm hours before you visit.

  • Gather permit and inspection records for additions, decks and converted space.
  • Keep the rental license, lease copies and security deposit ledger together for the buyer.
  • Ask the department how to confirm an unpermitted structure before it surprises a buyer's inspector.

What are the ways to sell an Edmonds house quickly?

Three routes cover most Edmonds situations, and the choice turns on condition, timeline and how much preparation you want to do.

  • A traditional listing: strong demand for views and walkable streets, but staging, showings and financing contingencies take time.
  • A direct sale to an investor or cash buyer: useful for dated houses, estate sales and tenant-occupied homes, with fewer repairs requested and a flexible closing date.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale: you keep the agent fee but carry the disclosure, negotiation and paperwork.

For an estate sale, ask the probate attorney whether the personal representative has the authority to sign before you accept an offer. For every route, compare offers by what you keep after the excise tax, any liens and the mortgage payoff.

What disclosures and excise tax come with an Edmonds sale?

For improved residential property, RCW 64.06.020 requires the seller to deliver a completed disclosure statement unless the buyer waived it or the transfer is exempt. Delivery is due within five business days of mutual acceptance unless the parties agree otherwise, and the buyer then has three business days to rescind. The form asks about title, water, sewer, structural issues and more, and it says to write NA rather than leave blanks.

The real estate excise tax is owed on the date of sale, which the Department of Revenue ties to the date the deed is signed before the notary, whatever the recording date. If the tax is not paid within one month, interest is charged from the date of sale, and the 2026 rate is 6 percent. Keep your sale records for at least four years, because the state can audit a sale and ask for support of the price or any exemption.

How do Snohomish County property taxes work for an Edmonds seller?

Snohomish County collects property tax in two installments, April 30 and October 31, and a statement should reach owners by March 15 under RCW 84.56.020. The October 31, 2026 second-half date has passed, so confirm it was paid. The next due date is April 30, 2027.

The county treasurer advises owners with a mortgage escrow to read escrow statements closely, since a payment collected at a refinance may not reach the treasurer until April or October. Mailed payments only need a postmark by the due date. Residential parcels with four or fewer units pay 9 percent annual interest on late taxes and no added penalty. The excise tax counter at the treasurer's office is open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.

What is the population of Edmonds, WA?

The Census Bureau estimates 42,748 residents as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census count was 42,853.

Do I need a business license to rent out a house in Edmonds?

Yes. The City of Edmonds treats home rentals as a General Business License, with a $186.87 application fee and a $74.75 annual renewal, filed through the state Department of Revenue system. Call Edmonds Business Licensing at 425-775-2525 with questions.

How long does an Edmonds seller have to give the buyer a disclosure statement?

Within five business days after mutual acceptance of the contract, unless the parties agree otherwise. The buyer then has three business days after delivery to rescind, under RCW 64.06.020. A buyer can waive the right to receive the form.

When is the Washington excise tax due on an Edmonds sale?

On the date of sale, paid to the county treasurer, with interest charged if it is not paid within one month. The state tiers start at 1.1 percent and rise to 1.28 percent above $525,000, plus a local rate. Sales beginning January 1, 2027 shift the first tier to $551,000.

Is Esperance part of Edmonds?

No. Esperance is an unincorporated area in the southeast corner that sits surrounded by Edmonds and has resisted annexation. Ask the county which jurisdiction handles permits and taxes for the address.

What should a seller know about Puyallup, Washington?

Puyallup is a Pierce County city on the Puyallup River, about 10 miles southeast of Tacoma and 35 miles south of Seattle. The Census Bureau estimates 42,682 residents as of July 1, 2025, a 0.7% dip from the April 2020 estimates base.

Ezra Meeker platted the townsite in 1877, and his hop farm drove growth through the 1880s until the town incorporated in 1890. Today the city is best known for the Washington State Fair, the state's largest annual fair. The city covers about 14 square miles of valley floor.

One detail trips up many sellers. Mailing addresses that say Puyallup also cover unincorporated areas such as South Hill, so check whether your parcel is inside city limits. That decides which permit office, zoning code and utility rules apply, while the county bills property tax either way.

What do the Census numbers say about Puyallup homes?

The Census puts Puyallup's median home value above $550,000 and its average commute above half an hour. The table collects the main QuickFacts figures.

How does Mount Rainier's lahar zone affect a Puyallup house?

Downtown Puyallup and nearby neighborhoods lie within a hazard zone for lahars, which are mudflows that a moderate or large Mount Rainier eruption could send down the Puyallup Valley. The city's rules respond to that risk. Under Puyallup Municipal Code 20.20.010(11)(L), accessory dwelling units are prohibited in the lahar exclusion area, with an exception for land within a half mile of the base of the surrounding elevation of the valley floor.

The city's September 2025 tip sheet explains what owners in that area can still do:

  • Build an addition or remodel that has an internal doorway and is not fully fire-wall separated from the main home.
  • Rent that added space to family or, if not family, to no more than one person.
  • Keep a guest house in a detached building, as long as it has no independent cooking facilities and no one lives there full time, with limited exceptions for family and employees.

If your house has a converted garage, a basement apartment or a backyard cottage, confirm with the Planning Division how the city treats it before you list. An unpermitted second unit can complicate a sale. Call 253-864-4165, option 3, or email Planning@PuyallupWA.gov.

What do Puyallup schools, roads and permits look like for a seller?

The Puyallup School District has 35 schools and serves more than 22,534 students, making it the ninth-largest district in the state. Its boundaries extend beyond the city to South Hill, parts of Tacoma and the Edgewood area. Pierce College Puyallup is a community college in the city.

State Routes 167 and 512 meet at Puyallup, giving freeway access toward Lakewood and the Green River Valley. Sounder commuter trains stop at Puyallup station on weekdays, and Pierce Transit buses and a microtransit zone that launched in 2023 serve the city.

The city Permit Center is on the second floor of City Hall at 333 South Meridian, with counter hours of 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and the main line is 253-864-4165. Anyone with an open building permit should ask the center to confirm its status.

How much real estate excise tax does a Puyallup seller owe?

The seller pays it under RCW 82.45.080, and the state portion is graduated. Through December 31, 2026, the rates are 1.1% up to $525,000, 1.28% from $525,000 to $1,525,000, 2.75% to $3,025,000 and 3% above. A local portion is added on top, which the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer can quote for your address.

For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue moves the thresholds to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. The Census median home value of $551,800 sits right at that new line. At that price, the state portion works out to about $6,118 under the 2026 brackets and about $6,071 under the 2027 brackets, a difference of roughly $47.

The sale date for tax purposes is the date the deed is notarized, not the recording date. The affidavit, deed and payment go to the county treasurer. After a payment, a refund request must be filed within four years of the sale and goes to the party who paid. See the Department of Revenue REET page.

How do Pierce County property taxes work at closing?

The first half of property tax is due April 30 and the second half by October 31. The county's FAQ says that because October 31 fell on a weekend in 2026, the second half was due Monday, November 2, a date that has now passed. A bill of $50 or less is due in full by April 30.

For residential property with one to four units, interest of 0.75% per month is charged on the full year's tax beginning May 1 if the first half is late, for tax year 2023 and later. You can still pay the first half plus interest through October 31. Ask your closing officer to settle any late amount from sale proceeds.

Pierce County values property at 100% of market value every year and physically inspects each property about once every six years. An owner who disagrees with the value may appeal to the Board of Equalization by July 1 of the assessment year or within 60 days of a value change notice, whichever is later. Only market value can be argued, not the size of the tax bill.

Seniors and people with disabilities may qualify for a property tax deferral. The state pays the tax, and the deferred amount becomes a lien that must be repaid with interest when ownership transfers, under RCW 84.38. If you hold a deferral, request a payoff figure early. The Assessor-Treasurer is at 2401 South 35th Street, Room 142, Tacoma, phone 253-798-6111.

What are the ways to sell a house in Puyallup?

A Puyallup owner can list the house, sell without an agent, or accept an as-is offer from a cash buyer. All three end with the same deed, excise tax affidavit and tax proration at closing.

  • A listing can reach the widest pool of buyers, with the time that showings and financing require.
  • An as-is offer suits a house with deferred repairs, an unpermitted unit or a conversion in the lahar zone.
  • Ask any buyer what they will pay for, who covers the excise tax, and when they want the deed notarized.

More questions about Puyallup, WA

Can I build a backyard cottage in Puyallup's lahar zone?

No. Puyallup Municipal Code 20.20.010(11)(L) prohibits accessory dwelling units in the lahar exclusion area, with an exception near the edge of the valley floor. A guest house with no independent cooking, not lived in full time, may be allowed.

When is the second half of Pierce County property tax due?

October 31, or the next business day if that date falls on a weekend. In 2026 it was Monday, November 2, which has passed. The next first-half date is April 30, 2027.

How much is the excise tax on a $551,800 Puyallup sale?

About $6,118 in state tax under the 2026 brackets, or about $6,071 if the sale takes place on or after January 1, 2027, before the local portion is added. The date the deed is notarized decides which brackets apply.

Does a South Hill address mean my house is in the city of Puyallup?

Not always. Puyallup mailing addresses cover adjacent unincorporated areas such as South Hill. Check your parcel with the city Planning Division or the county to confirm which rules apply.

What happens to a senior property tax deferral when I sell?

The amount the state paid on your behalf becomes a lien that is repaid, with interest, when ownership transfers. Request a payoff figure from the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer before closing.
